This involves reconstructing a signal characterized by group sparsity from an underdetermined system of equations. By leveraging this interpretation, the paper introduces a computationally efficient algorithm grounded in the group LASSO method. This proposed algorithm demonstrates superior performance compared to a benchmark that solves the group sparsity problem via conventional LASSO techniques. Additionally, the paper provides theoretical analysis to determine the conditions required for the exact recovery of group sparse vectors. Specifically, this study represents an initial effort to analyze the precise conditions for exact group sparse recovery using the group LASSO method. Simulations indicate that the proposed LMMI-based group LASSO algorithm can successfully identify sparse user groups even when the number of linear equations is significantly lower than the total number of users. Furthermore, the approach can effectively recover group sparse vectors when the count of equations is approximately twice the expected number of group sparse vectors, provided the minimum distance between group means is sufficiently large. These findings may aid in designing efficient algorithms for group sparse recovery applications. Finally, the paper includes a simulation example comparing the proposed group LASSO-based algorithm against a LASSO-based algorithm, demonstrating its improved performance over the LASSO-based approach. Additionally, it examines the performance of the proposed method against a benchmark multi-step algorithm that first identifies groups using group LASSO and then selects users within each identified group. Results from this comparison show that the multi-step algorithm outperforms the proposed LASSO-based algorithm. Additionally, the proposed LMMI-based algorithm exhibits greater robustness than the multi-LASSO-based algorithm when group sizes are incorrectly estimated. These findings are expected to facilitate the design of efficient algorithms for group sparse recovery applications. Simulation results also show that the proposed group sparsity-based algorithm performs comparably to another algorithm that jointly selects users and designs a precoder using MMSE-based methods. Finally, the precoder designed using the proposed group LASSO-based algorithm achieves significantly lower error rates than one designed using the conventional LASSO-based algorithm. These results confirm that the proposed group LASSO-based algorithm can effectively identify groups and design precoders to achieve the desired performance in group sparse recovery applications. The authors believe these findings will assist in designing precoders for group sparse recovery applications. Recent studies indicate that electronic correlations drive the breaking of both time-reversal and rotational symmetries, resulting in the sequential occurrence of antiferromagnetic and nematic orders, respectively, as the superconducting transition temperature is approached under decreasing carrier density. This review examines these concepts through the lens of a phenomenological two-fluid framework, which separates the superconducting order parameter into two distinct components: the conventional one arising from normal Coulomb interactions and a "counterflow" superconducting order linked to order parameter fluctuations. We find that the counterflow order, a concept first proposed in the context of superfluid helium, exhibits nodal symmetry and triggers the simultaneous collapse of superconductivity and nematic order as the superconducting gap vanishes at the nematic transition point. Consequently, we interpret experimental findings regarding nematic scattering of quasiparticles and the formation of nodes in the superconducting gap as evidence for counterflow superconductivity. Additionally, we explore various thermodynamic and transport properties, such as specific heat, thermal conductivity, and electrical and thermoelectric responses, supported by both theoretical calculations and available experimental data. Finally, we outline the implications of counterflow superconductivity for existing experimental results and suggest new proposals to clarify the underlying mechanisms. The proposed model offers a unifying framework that integrates diverse phenomena, including superconductivity, magnetic and nematic orders, and the emergence of anomalies in normal state transport, into a single theoretical structure. This paves the way for future experimental investigations to resolve longstanding controversies and deepening the understanding of these interwoven phenomena. Such insights could ultimately lead to the discovery of materials with higher transition temperatures and non-centrosymmetric superconductors displaying nematic states. The proposed flow-induced phenomena and the counterflow superconductivity model are anticipated to be relevant across a broad spectrum of physical systems. Furthermore, the theory may offer a framework for understanding the enigmatic Meissner effect in black holes, where the Meissner effect refers to the expulsion of magnetic fields. This counterflow superconductivity theory will be published in the Monograph Series of the Springer Series on Materials Research by Springer Nature. It synthesizes diverse phenomena into a unified theoretical framework. The authors anticipate that this comprehensive understanding will facilitate new experimental efforts to unravel the associated physical mechanisms. We incorporate the recently discovered tau lepton polarization data from the LHC to refine our findings. Given the potential for future lepton colliders to measure tau lepton properties with high precision, we examine how current data can be leveraged to predict outcomes at proposed machines like the ILC and CEPC. Our study covers the complete tau leon polarization dataset across seven scenarios, varying assumptions about the 2HDM mass spectrum and coupling structure. By combining experimental data with theoretical considerations, we derive more restrictive limits on the 2HDM parameter space. Our results demonstrate that the various 2HDM models can be distinguished from one another using this combined global fit analysis. Additionally, we show that tau lepton polarization data can help distinguish between the different 2HDM models. Ultimately, our analysis indicates that an ILD detector at the ILC will significantly enhance the study of the 2HDM model. quantum interference influences surface molecular self-assembly. This assembly is driven by the intramolecular orbital distribution and the lateral van der Waals interactions between molecules. Our findings indicate that while the intramolecular effect determines the initial molecular configuration, the intermolecular effect dictates that self-assembly is favorable when electronic orbitals exhibit high anisotropy. Conversely, these orbital effects can be overridden by intermolecular van der Waals interactions, which favor self-assembly in isotropic systems with strong interactions and an unfavorable intramolecular effect, or in anisotropic systems with weak interactions and a high intramolecular effect. The anisotropy of electronic orbitals can be adjusted through the work function of the substrate and the distance between molecules and the surface, allowing for the manipulation of surface self-assembly. Numerical results confirm the reliability of these theoretical predictions. As a specific example, we examined the deposition of C60 on Au(111) and found that our predictions align with existing experimental and theoretical data. This approach can be extended to other intramolecular effects and intermolecular forces. These insights may assist in the rational design of two-dimensional organic electronic devices and other functional materials. The method is validated through numerical simulations and \textit{ab-initio} calculations on both antiferromagnetic (AFM) and ferromagnetic (FM) CrI$_3$ monolayers. For the AFM material, we identify three magnon branches resulting from collective magnon-magnon interactions. In contrast, the FM case yields one flat band arising from magnon-magnon coupling. Our theoretical results align closely with the $\textit{ab-initio}$ findings for both chromium iodide variants. These findings indicate that the many-body framework for spin excitations in two-dimensional (2D) magnets must account for magnon-magnon interactions. This paves the way for creating spinon-phonon analogues using interacting magnons, enabling the potential generation of topological many-body spin excitations in coupled spin systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this same many-body approach applies to interacting electronic excitations in strongly correlated materials. These insights facilitate the design and fabrication of topological devices utilizing many-body spin excitations for next-generation information processing and storage systems. Additionally, our results offer a pathway to investigate the Haldane gap in 2D spin-1 systems. Finally, the proposed research framework serves as a foundation for exploring and manipulating the properties of topological many-body spin excitations in new quantum technologies. approach designed to train machine learning models without the necessity of transferring sensitive user data to a central server. Nevertheless, current FL methodologies are susceptible to privacy breaches, particularly when training involves a limited number of participants (referred to as the "small fleet" scenario). This scarcity of users hinders the model's generalizability, leading the server to incorporate user-specific data to maintain adequate performance standards. To address this issue, we propose the utilization of a generative adversarial network (GAN) to synthesize artificial data for training. By expanding the data volume through this artificial generation, the reliance on user-specific information is reduced, thereby mitigating privacy risks. Specifically, we investigate the application of federated GANs within a vertical setting to create missing data features. Furthermore, to ensure the integrity of the model generated through this artificial data, we employ data from a trusted source for the training process. This research demonstrates the viability of using a combination of real and artificial data to enhance the performance of small fleet federated learning systems while preserving user privacy. Additionally, to further safeguard against potential data leakage, we evaluate the application of the Apriori algorithm to analyze the contribution of each training sample to the final model. Our experimental findings indicate that the proposed method effectively prevents data leakage. This study aims to advance the real-world deployment of small fleet, privacy-preserving federated learning systems. Additionally, to broaden the applicability of our approach, we plan to expand the dataset used for training. Beyond the current implementation, future work will explore enhancing model performance by leveraging domain knowledge to generate more realistic artificial data. Specifically, we intend to incorporate medical knowledge to refine the quality of the synthesized data. Collectively, these efforts seek to further improve privacy protection and the overall performance of small fleet federated learning systems. posits that the observed baryon asymmetry in the universe is generated by the decay of $B$-mesons. This model extends the minimal supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) by including a charged lepton doublet and a singlet lepton from an ${\mathcal{SU}}(5)$ multiplet, alongside a complex scalar field also denoted as $\phi$. Lepton number violation arises from the $\phi$ field, with its mass scale determining the magnitude of this extension. During the decay of $B$-mesons, the final state is characterized by three leptons and three antileptons, yielding zero net lepton number. By assigning a mass of $\mathcal{O}(\text{GeV})$ to the $\phi$ field, its decay products (three leptons) are significantly more abundant than those of the next lightest particle, the muon. Consequently, events featuring three baryons alongside three muons become the most prominent channel, producing three protons. This configuration aligns with nucleogenesis and suggests a potential connection between the origins of baryon and baryon-like numbers. Furthermore, the model predicts a muon mass of approximately 1 GeV and anticipates that the three-lepton final state from $B$-mesons will exhibit non-uniformity or anomalous characteristics due to the $\phi$ field's influence. These aspects are being investigated in detail. The characteristic three-proton final state also offers an explanation for the "Peaks and Valleys" phenomenon observed in emulsion experiments traversed by ultra-high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs), a connection that motivates the study of the "Three-Proton Event" in these data. Additionally, the model predicts that the frequency of these three-proton events should vary with the $\phi$ field's mass, offering a method to constrain its value. Finally, the search for the $\phi$ field's mass is currently underway at the LHCb detector. This contribution will present the current status of these searches and related discussions. of a higher-dimensional AdS black hole surrounded by a photon gas within a quadratically modified gravity framework. Our findings indicate that the black hole's temperature declines as the photon gas density increases, causing the small black hole to collapse when the density becomes sufficiently high. Additionally, we analyzed the thermodynamic properties of the system using various state parameter values. These state parameter values were determined using a polynomial of the adiabatic index, accompanied by a brief discussion of the physical significance of these results. Finally, the study explores the Hawking--Page phase transition regarding the critical chemical potential. Through graphical analyses of both stable and unstable regions, we observed that the phase transition occurs at higher densities when the system is situated within the modified gravity regime. These results further demonstrate that the quadratically modified gravity term exhibits a similar behavior to the cosmological constant. Consequently, the research confirms that the black hole behaves analogously to an AdS black hole, with the phase transition occurring at higher densities as the AdS radius increases. Furthermore, for a fixed modified gravity parameter, increasing the dimensionality of the system causes the black hole to transition to a higher density regime as the AdS radius grows. In summary, the black--photon gas system within quadratically modified gravity displays behavior consistent with that in standard gravity. Consequently, our analysis of thermodynamic properties in this regime offers a significant contribution to the understanding of black hole physics. Finally, a discussion of the physical significance concludes this paper. (AuS-24-01) [51 pages, 14 figures]

Our method avoids the expensive forward and backward substitutions typically required by hierarchical solvers. Instead, it approximates the solution to the upwind block system (SBU) within the block lower-triangular system (SL) using a single iteration of the Jacobi method, followed by an explicit correction for the upper-block system (SBU+) in the block upper-triangular system (SU). We demonstrate that the SBU can be solved in one Jacobi iteration with a relative error of no more than 1%, with the maximum error occurring when diagonal matrix Aii is the slowest block to converge, yielding only a 2% deviation from the exact solution. Furthermore, the computational cost of our proposed approach is equivalent to performing a single Jacobi iteration on the SBU, representing approximately a 70% reduction in overhead compared to a full forward-backward substitution. ers on electron-electron interactions within the random field Ising model (RFIM), we observe that the screening of long-range Coulomb repulsion by collective spin fluctuations facilitates a screening-screened RFIM transition towards a paramagnetic phase. This transition is notably sensitive to the spatial dimensionality of the Coulomb repulsion when compared to the screening length of the spin-dependent random field. When the screening length approaches zero, the system undergoes a screening-dependent RFIM transition within spatial dimensionality $d=4+d_C$, where $d_C$ represents the Coulomb dimensionality. If the screening length is non-zero, the Coulomb dimensionality becomes a continuous one-dimensional function, resulting in a 5+$_{\ell}$-dimensional transition. In this scenario, the collective spin screening of the random field is characterized by a $1/r^6$-long-range Coulomb repulsion potential. Consequently, the critical behavior of the magnetization follows the standard RFIM scenario with an additional Coulomb dimensionality $d_C=2$, thereby reducing the critical exponent for the magnetization. Finally, this model scenario could be experimentally realized in a van der Waals ferromagnetic multilayer stack featuring randomly distributed impurities or defects with varying magnetic moments. In such a setup, the exchange repulsion between adjacent ferromagnetic layers would act as the random field, while a thin antiferromagnetic interlayer could introduce an effective Coulomb repulsion with a screening length that approaches zero as the thickness of the intercalated antiferromagnetic interlayer increases. In this specific case, the Coulomb dimensionality would be fixed at $d_C=4$.

However, existing literature typically concentrates solely on predicting future registrations or identifying at-risk students, neglecting the equally important task of analyzing past registrations. This paper introduces a model designed to recommend courses based on historical enrollment patterns. By treating past course selections as implicit feedback rather than explicit ratings, the approach avoids the biases inherent in rated data and offers a framework generalizable to other recommendation contexts involving implicit feedback. Although the recommended courses often share subjects with a student's prior coursework, the study investigates the benefits of incorporating the student's major into the recommendation model. The research question addresses why models relying solely on registration history may yield less accurate recommendations for students from specific majors compared to others. The study begins by reviewing prior research, followed by a recommendation model built on student registration history. It subsequently examines the influence of a student's major on historical data and explores methods to mitigate the resulting inaccuracies. Finally, the paper suggests potential avenues for future research regarding the application of past registrations. The study employs latent factorization, a method that represents items and users as vectors of latent features derived from their interactions. By representing both students and courses within a shared feature space, the model calculates similarity within this space to generate recommendations. Given that this research focuses on individual-level past registrations rather than group-based ones, a student's major serves merely as a filter for previously taken courses rather than a direct input to the model. This limitation can lead to inappropriate recommendations if a student from a particular major has taken courses outside their field of study. To address this, the paper investigates various methods for integrating the major into the recommendation process. It reviews several feature extraction techniques for majors and evaluates multiple approaches for merging major features with course representation vectors. Ultimately, it compares a model utilizing past registrations alone against one that incorporates both registration history and the major's feature vector. The comparison demonstrates that integrating the major alongside registration history improves recommendation accuracy. Furthermore, the study finds that while latent factorization produces recommendations sharing subjects with prior coursework, accurately predicting the student's major remains challenging when using only registration data, highlighting the necessity of additional major-specific features. This conclusion is supported by statistical tests confirming that incorporating the major's feature vector enhances recommendation accuracy. Future work could explore various methods for extracting features from student majors. Additionally, the study suggests that for individual-level registration analysis, including peers from the same major could further improve the accuracy of generated recommendations. automated vehicles (CAVs) within a mixed traffic environment containing both CAVs and human-driven vehicles (HDVs). The primary objective is to minimize the collective CAVs' travel time and fuel consumption while ensuring that HDVs experience only negligible performance disruption. To this end, we introduce a Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework that calculates a time-varying target speed profile, enabling each CAV to adjust its motion autonomously to pursue this shared goal. Crucially, the formulation incorporates constraints designed to prevent significant HDV interference and to ensure the formation's robustness against uncertain HDV behaviors. Specifically, the algorithm ensures that HDVs following CAVs are not severely impeded, allowing for explicit evaluation of the formation's robustness with respect to each specific HDV. Numerical simulations demonstrate the approach's effectiveness and highlight the benefits gained by accounting for the vehicle-specific characteristics of all road users involved. Furthermore, the study explores the impact of looking-ahead distance on CAVs and the uncertainty associated with HDVs on mixed traffic lanes, revealing that increased looking-ahead distances significantly reduce total travel time for CAVs and enhance the traffic's overall robustness. Additionally, the analysis indicates that the specific remapping strategy and communication frequency of CAVs have minimal influence on the overall results. Finally, the MPC approach proves highly effective, successfully delivering the desired performance despite the presence of HDVs and varying road conditions. These findings offer a robust foundation for the practical deployment of highway CAV platooning systems. To better understand and mitigate these errors, we analyze SGD through a continuous-time framework known as a transport equation. Unlike conventional approaches that formulate solutions via the forward equation, we employ the more advanced Lagrangian view to derive the solution using the method of characteristics. We contrast this forward-backward pair and argue that the Lagrangian perspective offers superior insight into the evolution of initial conditions along their trajectories. Furthermore, we apply this viewpoint to examine the convergence of SGD. standard approach for analyzing time-to-event data in oncology randomized controlled trials. This method estimates treatment effects specifically at the final time point. This study examines the implications of this limitation and proposes an extension of the MMRM framework designed to evaluate treatment effects on time-to-event outcomes across all time points. The efficacy of this proposed framework is assessed using simulated data generated from the relapse prevention setting of a 2x2 trial involving a theoretical immunotherapy and chemotherapy for non-small cell lung cancer. Model fitting was performed using SAS 9.4's PROC MIXED. An analysis-decision utility (ADU) was calculated for each model to compare the utility of the MMRM extension against the standard MMRM. An ADU was also computed by excluding the primary endpoint from the MMRM analysis. An additional analysis compared both MMRM approaches against the standard log-rank test, which utilizes imputed times. Results indicated that the MMRM extension outperformed the standard MMRM when analyzing all time points, although the statistical significance varied by dataset. When the final time point was included in the analysis, no significant difference in ADU was observed between the two MMRM approaches across all datasets. Consequently, the study concludes that the MMRM extension serves as a robust method for analyzing time-to-event data in randomized controlled trials when the final time point is the primary focus; however, extending the analysis to all time points remains an area for future investigation. Additionally, the study suggests that handling censoring and ensuring appropriate model specification are critical factors in MMRM analysis. (Sponsor's Statement))

a significant challenge, primarily because of inter-robot interactions. While safety is typically achieved by maintaining specific obstacle-free zones around each robot, known as Safety Distance Sets (SDS), the dynamic nature of these sets creates conflicts that necessitate precise temporal coordination to enable conflict-free flight paths. However, the existence of a conflict-free solution is not guaranteed a priori due to the complex, time-dependent interactions between moving SDS. To address this, we introduce a novel methodology that approximates the existence region for conflict-free trajectories as a Conflicts-Free Existence Region (CFER). Defined as a subset of the configuration space-time, the CFER serves as a conflict-free box in configuration space for every robot state, allowing the verification of conflict-free existence by checking if the system resides within it. Since the solution space for conflict-free existence is often high-dimensional, we propose utilizing a dimensionality reduction technique called Topological Data Analysis (TDA). We demonstrate that TDA can generate a one-dimensional persistence diagram (PD) from a given SDS and effectively represent the confounding factors that prevent a solution from residing within the CFER. Furthermore, under specific assumptions regarding SDS properties, a PD within the t-space of a single robot's configuration state can predict whether a multi-robot solution exists in the t-space of the overall configuration state. Finally, experimental results on a multi-robot system confirm the efficacy of our proposed approach. The entire methodology, from ConfDS-Existence Region (CFER) to PD generation and E-commerce, is open-source and available for implementation. The papers are currently under review. Typically, TSL systems rely on an ASR-generated list of the top-N hypotheses to infer semantic meaning, extract acoustic features, and track the dialogue state. However, ASR systems frequently contain errors, leading to misinterpretation of TSL features and mis-tracking of the dialogue state. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a TSL-based attention model that utilizes an error-driven approach to enhance TSL feature extraction. The model first determines the highest hypothesis among the top-N ASR hypotheses. Subsequently, it computes a weighted average of the encoded features from the remaining N-1 hypotheses to enhance the overall TSL feature extraction. This model effectively addresses the limitations of ASR systems and is both computationally efficient and easy to implement. The proposed approach has achieved new state-of-the-art results on the 2020 CISL benchmark. The source code is available at: https://github.com/zhaoqian712/TSL-based-Attention-Model. One prominent method, OneShot, utilizes a neural network to generate single edits intended to fix programs directly. In contrast, our proposed framework, TreeRepair, integrates program patches with a set of constraints derived from failing test cases. These constraints utilize match statements to identify specific locations within the source code where test failures occur. Unlike OneShot, which relies on a single edit, TreeRepair generates a collection of edits to achieve the necessary fixes. We enhanced this collection by incorporating both program text and control-flow graphs as input features for our model. Furthermore, we introduced a post-processing step that eliminates redundant edits from the collection. Experimental results on the BigBen dataset demonstrate that, on average, TreeRepair requires fewer edits and executes post-processing logic more frequently than OneShot, leading to both higher success and higher success-at-first-guess rates. Additionally, we conducted a user study in collaboration with practitioners to assess success rates and gather qualitative feedback regarding the repaired programs.

For the second, we develop a novel one-dimensional stoichiometric stoichiometric chemostat model, extending prior work on invasive species, specifically the Dynamic Energy Budget (DEB) model. This extension leverages our flow analysis to create a non-Newtonian-extended Stokes system for mimicking mucous secretion by mussels to enhance dispersal. We provide numerical simulations to illustrate the effects of this proposed extension. Overall, this work signifies a substantial advancement in mathematical modeling, enabling the simultaneous modeling of fluid dynamics, various spatial scales, and biovolume. Such capabilities are particularly valuable for applied fields like environmental mechanics and multiphase flow. Furthermore, this integration of fluid dynamics and biovolume paves the way for simulating species interactions using a single model. These findings were presented at the Mathematics of Infectious Diseases 2021 conference. Additionally, the associated repository contains a video showcasing the videos featured in this article. \section{Introduction}

Data distribution shift is a prevalent challenge in numerous learning applications. For instance, in image classification, the training images may originate from a different domain than the testing images, representing a classic instance of distribution shift. Another prevalent scenario involves scenarios where the data generation process is unknown, making it impossible to access the true data distribution; in such cases, one can only sample from the training dataset, creating a distribution shift between the true data and the sampled samples. These scenarios are particularly significant because empirical risk minimization (ERM) is prone to failure when there is a distribution shift between training and testing data. This paper specifically investigates how SGD trained on a single training dataset can adapt to the true data distribution in the absence of prior knowledge about the data generation process.

a novel approach for detecting and correcting "stuck-at" faults within 32-bit adders used in 28-nm FPGA logic.

**Methodology:** Faulty adders are identified by comparing their sum outputs against those of a healthy adder, utilizing a new technique for aligning binary representations. Corrections are implemented by constructing a Truth Table that maps current adder outputs to the expected results of a functional unit.

**Results:** A 28-nm FPGA was employed to design a diagnostic module with an 800 MHz operating frequency. The module successfully constructs a correction table and achieves diagnostic coverage (DC) values ranging from 96.875% to 100%.

**Conclusion:** Empirical evidence indicates that this method is highly effective for identifying and remediating "stuck-at" faults in 32-bit adders on 28-nm FPGAs. Furthermore, the approach is applicable to other 32-bit adder types and can be integrated into the design stage to enhance reliability and operational efficiency. Finally, the methodology is suitable for implementation in 7nm FPGAs, provided appropriate adjustments are made. We say that $f$ and $g$ are in *general position* if the preimages $f^{-1}(0)$ and $g^{-1}(0)$ intersect in a manner that is as transverse as possible. This article characterizes this configuration using Vilarino's function. As an application, we determine which functions reside in the same orbit under the action of all point transformations of the plane that preserve the Crasta curve $z=e^y$. Furthermore, we divide the space of submersion functions from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}$ into orbits based on whether they are in general position with respect to $z=e^y$. The cardinalities of these orbits provide a complete invariant for the rank 1 feedback linearizable system $\dot{x}=ax+by$, where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. Consequently, we provide a characterization of such systems up to point transformation. Finally, we offer an open cover of the parameter space of rank 1 feedback linearizable systems, with each component of the cover representing a distinct orbit. These results advance the characterization of rank 1 multi-input systems in two dimensions and may be extended to higher dimensional cases. Additionally, we provide a full description of the Crasta manifold $M_f = \{p \in \mathbb{R}^2 : f(p)=0 \text{ and } \mathrm{d}f(p)=0\}$ for a submersion function $f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$. We demonstrate that $M_f$ consists of a union of analytic submanifolds of dimension at most 1, where each manifold lies within a single connected component. By computing the differential $dV_f$ on $M_f$, we derive a complete characterization of a submersion function $f$ based on the properties of its zero set $M_f$, its manifold dimensions, and the value of $dV_f$ on each component. To facilitate this, we present a formula for $dV_f$ along $M_f$ involving the rank of the Hessian matrix of $f$. To the author's knowledge, no fully explicit differential invariant for submersion functions in the plane has previously been established. While prior research has mainly focused on approximating convex functions and projections, this paper introduces a novel approach to approximating the median of a random variable. Specifically, the analysis demonstrates that applying a randomized projection using $O(d/\varepsilon^2)$ measurements allows for the accurate estimation of the $\tau$-median of a vector, where $\varepsilon$ represents the target error level and $d$ denotes the desired dimensionality of the sketch. Consequently, this technique allows for the highly parallel estimation of up to $d$ quantiles within a constant number of passes over the data. The core innovation relies on a technique known as random cropping, which is also a component of the median of means method. Furthermore, the proposed approach is general enough to support the estimation of the $\tau$-quantile and a broad range of other entry-wise functions. The framework includes a method for estimating the mean using constant numbers of passes over the input vector. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of this approach, which expands the capabilities of CountSketch and offers a superior alternative to the widely popular Local Sensitivity Sketch (LSS) for estimating quantiles. Additionally, the framework is more robust than LSS when handling updates to individual vector entries. The implementation is available at https://github.com/andrewdp/median-sketch. MedianSketch surpasses both the theoretical performance and empirical outcomes of LSS, as well as the state-of-the-art bit vector-based algorithm, QuantSketch. A comprehensive comparison with state-of-the-art methods, alongside a detailed analysis of theoretical guarantees and empirical results, is provided in the appendix. The code is accessible at https://github.com/andrewdp/median-sketch.

This approach was inspired by the Kripke-Joyal correspondence in sheaf topos theory and executed through three distinct stages. The first stage defined a category of predomes—sets of propositions structured like posets—but with elements representing evidence for entailment rather than the entailments themselves. The second stage utilized the presheaf construction to transform these predomes into topological spaces, termed "hats." The final stage involved mapping these hats into a topos, specifically one containing sheaves. The paper's novel contribution lies in its focus on the first stage; while semantic models exist at both the hats and topos levels, no formalization of predomes or maps between them has previously appeared in the literature. Consequently, this work aims to fill that gap by defining predomes and exploring continuous functions between them, which constitute the primary innovation. Furthermore, the paper explores a novel proposal to initiate a second realization of the hats-to-topos step within HoTTpy, a functional programming language based on Homotopy Type Theory (HoTT) that integrates Coq and Agda's features. Initiating this proposal early in the research process is intended to highlight the nature of topoi and sheaves and underscore the potential of HoTTpy as a platform for further exploring the Kripke-Joyal correspondence. Additionally, the discussion will address the broader significance of this correspondence and its potential integration with HoTTpy. Finally, the paper will highlight how HOmOTopy Type Theory Pyton (HoTTpy) serves as a valuable medium for such investigations, combining visual intuition with type theory and functional programming to foster new perspectives on these concepts. This approach is especially valuable given that Kripke models for first-order logic have already been formalized in HOmOTopy Type Theory (HoTT), a language that also integrates Coq and Agda's capabilities. HOmOTopy Type Theory Pyton offers an accessible entry point for this material, providing simpler type theory and functional programming features that facilitate understanding. Key points covered include an overview of Kripke models and their extension to sheaf topos theory, an explanation of why HOmOTopy Type Theory Pyton is an effective starting point for this discussion, and an overview of Kripke models through the lens of HOmOTopy Type Theory Pyton. The outcome is expected to be enhanced understanding and visualization of Kripke models and their extension to sheaf topos theory via HOmOTopy Type Theory Pyton.

Our primary finding is that dust-to-gas ratio variations within dense clouds significantly impact Sub-millimeter dust emission maps. Consequently, when both dust and gas data are accessible, the Sub-millimeter dust-to-gas ratio should not be assumed to remain constant at 0.01 across star-forming regions. Applying this method to Taurus A and B, Chamaeleon I, and Ophiuchus A & B reveals that the average dust-to-gas ratio in these regions falls between 0.003 and 0.005. In contrast, the dust-to-gas ratio in the Perseus and Aquila Cruxa regions is approximately 0.008. These values are notably lower than the typical value of 0.01 often assumed for star-forming regions. Our results align with recent observations indicating that the cosmic dust budget exceeds the amount expected from the gas reservoir by a factor of three to four. We conclude by discussing the origins of this missing dust within the context of the dust lifecycle. Specifically, we propose that the destruction of interstellar dust grains in the hot phase exceeds their creation in the cold phase, leading to a net loss of cosmic dust. This process may account for the observed discrepancy in the dust budget. We outline the subsequent steps required to test this hypothesis. Ultimately, this research may contribute to resolving the long-standing issue of the missing dust problem. We hope that our findings will inspire further investigation into the origin of the missing dust puzzle. We look forward to the next step of this study. we investigate the connection between initial geometric anisotropies and anisotropic flow in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV. Specifically, we examine how initial spatial and initial momentum anisotropies scale with centrality between these two systems. By analyzing the Cu+Cu data, which exhibits a stronger systematics deviation from ideal hydrodynamic behavior, we estimate the anisotropies that a perfect fluid would generate. Our results demonstrate a near-linear relationship between $e_2$, $e_3$, and $e_4$ (the anisotropies) along with $v_2\{2\}$, $v3\{2\}$, and v4\{2\} (the anisotropic flow coefficients) across all centrality classes. The consistency between the Cu+Cu and Au+Au results supports the validity of our methodology. Additionally, by calculating the ratio of anisotropic flow coefficients to the squared eccentricity ($e_2^2$), we find that the anisotropic flow generated by a perfect fluid is suppressed by a factor of approximately 2 to 3 compared to the initial geometric anisotropy. Finally, we compare our findings with recent experimental data and theoretical models based on ideal and viscous hydrodynamics. These results suggest that the suppression of anisotropic flow relative to initial eccentricity is primarily caused by viscosity, which is consistent with the more viscous environment expected in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV. This conclusion is also reinforced by the Cu+Cu data. Overall, these results provide strong evidence for the significant impact of viscosity on the evolution of the quark-gluon plasma created in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV. Furthermore, by employing a graded extension of Quillen–Suslin theory, we establish a corresponding result for graded rings. As a direct consequence, we demonstrate that these groups vanish for locally bounded rings, which encompasses Noetherian rings. In the specific case of Bass nil-groups of order $n$ for unitary groups, we provide a direct computation; however, we do not address the more complex scenario involving Bak's unitary groups. Additionally, we examine the connection between these groups and Bass's higher algebraic $K$-groups in non-connected rings, a relationship that appears to exist exclusively with Bak's unitary groups. Finally, we establish a link between NK-groups and $K$-groups by presenting a non-trivial example in positive dimension where the unitary group $U_2$ exhibits infinite 2-torsion. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first established example of Nakasato-type phenomena, a term coined by Antieau and Dugger to describe the absence of higher algebraic $K$-group torsion under certain conditions that hold in lower dimensions or for lower suspensions. This phenomenon was previously identified by Antieau and Dugger for graded polynomial rings and later for regular local rings of dimension at least 3. To our knowledge, this work introduces the phenomenon for the first time in rings that are not Noetherian. To our surprise, the phenomenon also arises in the context of NK-groups. To address the resulting complexity, we propose a general conjecture and attempt to formulate a conjectural explanation for the phenomenon by utilizing Geller and Sridharan's theory of algebraic $K$-theory for graded rings. Specifically, we define the nil-property for a graded ring as the absence of positive-dimensional NK-groups and define the $n$-nil property as the absence of $n$-torsion in these groups. Leveraging Geller and Sridharan's theory, we prove that the nil-property holds for graded rings where every standard slice is either a field or a principal ideal ring. This result generalizes the findings of Geller and Sridharan and establishes the absence of positive-dimensional NK-groups for graded valuation rings and graded valuation domains. Consequently, we confirm that these groups are absent for locally bounded rings and certain Henselian rings. We define

We introduce a new class of PEAs termed cloud-based PEAs (cPEAs), which substitute the single host architecture of traditional PEAs with a host–slave model to boost both computational power and task parallelism. This study examines two cPEA configurations: a conventional master–slave architecture and a novel hierarchical multi-level multi-task parallelism model called the task tree. The efficacy of these cPEA variants was evaluated across four distinct problem domains. While their performance relative to standard PEAs is evident, the task tree model demonstrated superior operation time and parallel speedup characteristics compared to the traditional master–slave approach. Furthermore, the task tree's performance relative to its hierarchical predecessor, the deep recurrent artificial life system (DRALS), was also assessed, revealing significant improvements in parallel speedup. Finally, the study provides an in-depth analysis of the task tree model's performance characteristics, exploring the interplay between algorithmic and system design decisions. This analysis underscores the critical impact of the degree of task decomposition on the overall efficacy of the cPEA task tree model.

17-BLG-1040 was recently confirmed as hosting a super-Earth planet with a mass of $M_p = 3.4 M_\oplus$ orbiting a stellar primary of mass $M_s = 0.19 M_\odot$, distinguished by its uniquely long orbital separation of $a_{sp} = 1.34$ AU. To evaluate the stability of such a planetary system, we examine two scenarios: one where the planet is the sole member of the system, and another where it resides within a multi-planet architecture. Our analysis indicates that a single planet at $1.34$ AU lies well within the stable region of a $0.19 M_\odot$ star, provided the Hill sphere is appropriately defined for low-mass stars. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a circumstellar configuration comprising two planets ($M_{p1} = 3.4 M_\odot$ and $M_{p2} = 1.55 M_\odot$) separated by $1.34$ AU is also viable. Additionally, we identify a broader stable zone encompassing $M_\odot$-wide separation between the planets, contingent upon the primary's mass. These findings underscore that super-Earth planets around low-mass stars can maintain stable orbits even at wide separations. Furthermore, new $\mu$SR and NMR measurements indicate that below 10% Co doping, local magnetism persists down to temperatures near absolute zero. These findings collectively demonstrate that ferromagnetism is not a robust characteristic of this system. The depolarization data can be interpreted using a competition between ferromagnetic and nematic long-range orders, consistent with existing literature. Additionally, the extrapolation of local magnetism measurements to zero temperature suggests that frustrated fluctuations of local moments may exist in the ground state of both nematic and ferromagnetic phases. Overall, these results provide fresh insights into the complex ferromagnetism of FeSi-based superlattices and its dependence on valence electron concentration. Finally, the paper discusses how these results align with theoretical models of ferromagnetism in this system, along with an analysis of theoretical valence electron concentrations for FeSi and FeSi$_3$. These conclusions reinforce the view that ferromagnetism in FeSi is an emergent, doping-tunable local magnetism arising from specific electronic and magnetic exchange interactions. Furthermore, the observed suppression of ferromagnetism in the superlattice phase supports the hypothesis that nematicity plays a crucial role in establishing long-range ferromagnetic order in FeSi. This hypothesis is also supported by the observation of ferromagnetism in nematic V$_x$Fe$_{1-x}$Si, which shares a superatomic electronic structure with FeSi. Consequently, these findings offer a fresh perspective on the nature of ferromagnetism in FeSi. In conclusion, the discovery of ferromagnetism in V$_x$Fe$_{1-x}$Si, combined with the tunable ferromagnetism in Fe$_{1-x}$Co$_x$Si/FeSi$_3$ superlattices, indicates that ferromagnetism in FeSi is an emergent local magnetism that is nematic-driven and easily adjustable via electronic structure modifications. (HI) observations offer a promising method for studying the gravitational potential of dwarf galaxies. This study reports 21 cm HI observations of the low-mass galaxy M32, which are among the most sensitive and highest-resolution HI data obtained for a galaxy with a stellar mass of $M_* \sim 10^8$ M$_{\odot}$. The observations reveal a clear HI disk extending to approximately 1.5 kpc, with a gas mass of $M_{HI} \sim 10^6$ M$_{\odot}$ and a gas-to-stellar mass ratio of $M_{HI}/M_* \sim 0.1$. This ratio is comparable to those seen in higher-mass galaxies and significantly exceeds the ratio predicted by the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation. The HI disk exhibits a deprojected rotation velocity of $v_{rot} \sim 30$ km s$^{-1}$ and an HI disk inclination of $i \sim 25^{\circ}$. De-rotated HI intensity profiles indicate a circular rotation curve that flattens at a distance of roughly 0.5 kpc, suggesting a total mass of $M_{tot} \sim 10^8$ M$_{\odot}$. This mass is notably lower than the total mass of $M_{tot} \sim 3-4 \times 10^8$ M$_{\odot}$ derived from kinematic studies of globular clusters. We conclude that the discrepancy between these estimates is due to the dominant dark matter halo in the globular cluster data experiencing significant radial anisotropy.

This challenge is particularly critical in cross-lingual settings because source and target languages often differ significantly, particularly in semantic richness and phonotactic constraints. Current research predominantly relies on model-based learning strategies that train GNNs alongside a generative adversarial network (GAN) using a min-max framework. However, this approach suffers from two primary drawbacks: first, it is limited to static test-time scenarios and fails to address dynamic learning situations; second, it typically requires a complete and high-quality graph structure, which is often unavailable in real-world deployments. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a test-time graph completion mechanism paired with a text-based graph GAN. 9-4802.7, located approximately 1.2 kpc from the Galactic center, consists of a white dwarf with a mass of 0.57 solar masses orbiting a black hole of 1.3 solar masses. Its orbital period of 10.1 days classifies it as the tightest known binary system containing a black hole and a white dwarf. The white dwarf's surface temperature of 22,000 K and its 7.5 Earth masses suggest it is a heavy helium giant that has undergone significant mass loss. Hydrodynamic simulations of the final common envelope phase indicate that the black hole and this helium giant were once much closer, with an orbital period of only 0.02 days. Furthermore, modeling suggests the helium giant was on its way to a merger when it was ejected from the envelope. The system's close separation and the giant's advanced evolutionary stage imply that RXCJ0232.9-4802.7 is a frequent product of common envelope evolution. Future observations with the TESS mission are expected to detect many similar systems, potentially revealing ultrashort orbital periods that could be attributed to common envelope ejection. Additionally, the system's orbital period is short enough that the black hole X-ray emission is detectable by Chandra and XMM-Newton, with variability expected due to the accretion disk's interaction with the donor star. The authors conclude that RXCJ0232.9-4802.7 serves as a valuable prototype for understanding the final common envelope phase.

Neural Network, is suggested as a potent approach for addressing any reversible chemical reaction within computed molecular systems. This network leverages learned Legendre Legendre transformation pairs of thermodynamic potentials to represent molecular state changes under varying electric or magnetic fields, as well as adiabatic or quasi-adiabatic mechanical conditions. By employing suitable Hamiltonian and/or free energy functions of molecular coordinates and momenta (or equivalent mixed variables) within a symmetric dual representation, the Legendre Neural Network generates a reliable state-transition operator (or a pair of such operators) capable of simulating the evolution of an inverse reaction simply by reversing the sign of the Legendre neural Hamiltonian (or free-energy) layers. Consequently, the network is applicable to any molecular reaction involving charged or magnetic molecules, or both, provided reactions involving direct nuclear motion are excluded. Furthermore, a numerical case study on the ESR spectrum of the CH radical is conducted, demonstrating that the Legendre Neural Network achieves high-precision modeling of paramagnetic paramagnetic transitions and magnetic resonance phenomena. Consequently, the network is also well-suited for simulating both MRS and QMRS spectra. A future extension utilizing the Legendre Neural Network approach could involve the development of a Legendre neural linear response function framework, which would enable the computation of free-energy-based response functions and the associated response functions derived from their Legendre transforms. This would facilitate the accurate modeling of linear response functions linked to the Legendre-transformed free energy (Kubo free energy) and the resulting response functions, which can be calculated via the second method of Legendre transforms, specifically KMS or Wigner-type correlations. In conclusion, the Legendre Neural Network offers a promising tool for comprehensively and reliably simulating the reversible connections between molecular reactions and molecular spectroscopy. Future research will focus on deeply investigating the various characteristics of the Legendre Neural Network and its applications in chemical and biological fields. Additionally, the potential for employing a quantum version of the network, the Quantum Legendre Neural Network, to model both MRS and QMRS is briefly discussed. Finally, it is proposed that the findings from this study will significantly contribute to the future development of computational methods for numerically calculating the various spectroscopic properties of molecules and biological entities. The accompanying source code is available at https://github.com/ymatsuzawa/Legendre-Neural-Network. A primary candidate for dark matter is the weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP), yet the lack of definitive experimental results has prompted a re-evaluation of WIMP searches using novel techniques and advanced concepts. This paper outlines the current status of WIMP investigations and explores several novel search strategies, while also addressing issues related to the fine-tuning problem. Current experimental progress indicates that the WIMA paradigm remains viable, although the future discovery timeline may be delayed. This delay could be mitigated through the use of novel search concepts and the incorporation of advanced particle physics model features. Ultimately, as we enter the LHC's high-luminosity era and a new generation of dedicated dark matter experiments, we anticipate promising new directions for WIMP research. is deeply rooted in human experience, and non-native speakers often encounter significant difficulties when acquiring a new language. These challenges stem from the need to master vast amounts of new information and align it with pre-existing knowledge. To alleviate this cognitive burden, researchers are exploring the concept of language transfer—the application of relevant knowledge from a first language (L1) to a second language (L2). This study investigates transfer learning as a methodology for leveraging L1 knowledge to facilitate L2 acquisition. Specifically, it examines how topic models can be employed to model and transfer relevant knowledge from the L1 to the L2. The research begins by outlining a framework for applying topic model-based transfer learning, followed by an analysis of its performance using two datasets: two languages closely related within the Indo-European family, and two that are distantly related. Results indicate that this approach successfully transfers knowledge from L1 to L2, particularly for long-tail topics, whereas direct model training without transfer yields poor performance. Consequently, this study demonstrates that utilizing CTF and document-level transfer within topic modeling enhances the accuracy of modeling L2 distributions and significantly improves transfer performance for long-tail topics. Finally, the document demonstrates that language pairs exhibiting greater similarity yield more effective knowledge transfer. These findings underscore the potential of transfer learning in topic model-based document classification and information retrieval, suggesting that L1 knowledge can be effectively transferred to L2 users to reduce the complexity of learning a new language and accelerate the process. We demonstrate that this representation projectivity equates to the projectivity of the group algebras they contain. Assuming the Kervaire dimension of the group action is at most one, we characterize the projectivity of a group action through the projectivity of its restriction to a central subgroup relative to the pointwise fixed field. Consequently, we derive criteria for the projectivity of linear group actions, contingent upon the existence of a core of codimension at most one. Hoare logic serves as a formalism for formal verification, capable of verifying programs' correctness and reliability and integrating with verification tools like Coq and Isabelle/HOL through intermediate representation formats such as Gallina and star logic. These frameworks rely heavily on carefully defined pre- and postconditions expressed as logical predicates. While temporal logics like TLTL have been developed to specify program behaviors involving time, their intricate nature often complicates the definition of appropriate predicates for verification tasks. This study introduces a novel temporal logic tailored for formal verification that simplifies the specification of specifiable behaviors. By utilizing vector clocks, the logic effectively models the relative time ordering of events, which is crucial for ensuring consistency. Furthermore, the proof rules for this new logic are designed to be user-friendly and compatible with the deduction capabilities of existing pre- and postconditions. Finally, the study demonstrates that the specified logic can be monotonically embedded into an existing logic, thereby allowing the development of verification tools to utilize the new logic without requiring additional engineering efforts. The vector clock mechanism also proves valuable for verifying concurrent programs by accounting for event ordering. Additionally, the paper provides a detailed proof of the specification logic's soundness using an existing verification tool. This soundness proof underscores both the rigorous development process and the proof capabilities of the intermediate logic. Consequently, the work introduces a new, efficient way to specify relative time behavior of programs, facilitating both sequential and concurrent validation, and enables the development of verification tools using the embedded logic. This approach allows tools to verify not only sequential but also concurrent programs with enhanced efficiency. To validate the proposed logic's utility, the study successfully verifies two real-world programs using the created tools. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the new logic is more efficient than its predecessor, highlighting the practical advantages of the logic designed in this work. Additionally, the study addresses a critical issue regarding the correct definition of a temporal logic, clarifying the necessity of vector clocks and the nuances of predicate semantics. This research paves the way for future work, including generalizing the logic for broader applications and further refining proof methodologies. Ultimately, the paper shows that temporal logics can be effectively integrated with the star logic framework, enabling verification via the developed tools. Moreover, the study confirms that both the temporal and spatial aspects of a logic can be independently and effectively integrated, opening avenues for future enhancements to the logic framework. distributed systems, such as blockchains and key-value stores. Contemporary algorithms, such as PBFT and its derivatives, often rely on synchronous or quasi-synchronous communication assumptions to ensure safety; however, these assumptions are frequently violated in practical environments, particularly in fault-tolerant cryptocurrency systems where safety is critical. Specifically, the current consensus mechanism for Bitcoin Core may fail under asynchronous conditions even with an honest majority, as demonstrated by the RLB attack. This paper introduces a novel transaction confirmation mechanism for Bitcoin Core that (i) minimizes latency for confirmed transactions delivered to the network and (ii) guarantees safety in fully asynchronous networks with an honest majority. Latency is measured by the number of mined blocks required for a high-probability confirmation, which is analyzed in terms of hash rate distribution, network delays, and miner adversarial behavior. Furthermore, the study outlines the necessary changes to Bitcoin Core's current transaction confirmation mechanism to support these performance and safety enhancements. Additionally, the paper presents an updated version of Heir of Bitcoin, a research tool that models Bitcoin Core specifically for analyzing such changes. Finally, the work discusses the potential of these proposed mechanisms when integrated into future blockchain systems designed from the ground up to support asynchronous networks.

of lipid bilayers, derived from neutron spin echo and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) relaxation techniques involving linear transport properties, have sparked significant debate regarding the appropriate analysis methods and underlying assumptions. To address these discrepancies and provide a more robust interpretation of existing data, we introduce a model utilizing an unsymmetrical Rouse framework for lateral diffusion within bilayers. This model incorporates a generalized memory function that links to specific relaxation time scales, allowing for independent determination of micro- and macro-diffusion time scales and the spatial distribution of cholesterol within lipid bilayers. Furthermore, the model examines how varying cholesterol bending moduli influence these observations. Our analysis of current literature data indicates that to align with recent measurements of cholesterol's effect on bending moduli, NMR relaxation studies must demonstrate size-dependent self-diffusion for probe molecules. However, because recent reports of cholesterol effects in shear viscosity—based on proton NMR and rotating frame dispersion techniques relying on collective transport properties—contradict this requirement, we conclude that the currently accepted values for cholesterol's bending modulus remain unverifiable. This discrepancy may stem from an inappropriate application of the Stokes-Einstein relation in prior studies. Consequently, we propose future investigations employing independent methods to directly measure both the bending modulus and surface viscosity of cholesterol-containing lipid bilayers. Furthermore, simulations utilizing independent charging techniques could help clarify the specific roles of headgroup dipoles and tailgroup van der Waals forces in the presence of cholesterol. Finally, extending this research to more complex, physiologically relevant lipid compositions could yield critical insights into cellular membrane behavior. These unresolved issues highlight the necessity for more rigorous and comprehensive studies to establish definitive values for the bending moduli of cholesterol-enriched lipid bilayers. Additionally, we provide a detailed examination of the central binomial coefficient, yielding novel asymptotic results for this and related functions. These methods are also anticipated to be applicable for isolating constant terms in asymptotic expansions of combinatorial sums involving Legendre polynomials, a question addressed in this paper with respect to those polynomials. Ultimately, the proposed EGF-based rewriting framework is versatile and can be extended to other areas, such as the constant term analysis for counts of combinatorial objects derived from coefficient extraction from multiple power series. Consequently, this approach promises to be a valuable tool for researchers in combinatorics. Key concepts include rewriting, asymptotics, combinatorial sums, generating functions, and constant terms. We argue that, unless quantum mechanics is revised, this experiment, like others involving macroscopically distinct yet microscopically equivalent quantum states, must yield indistinguishable measurement outcomes. This conclusion remains valid whether one adopts the standard interpretation or the unitary approach advanced by Penrose and Hameroff. Consequently, the configuration fails to illustrate the quantum erasure of macroscopic entanglement. Furthermore, among the various arguments the group offers to reconcile their experiment with the predictions of quantum mechanics, only the claims regarding nonlinear amplification and the spontaneous collapse of the wave function are viable. Finally, we offer an alternative proposal to showcase the quantum interference of macroscopically distinct, originally macro-entangled quantum states. This can be achieved using existing technology by employing two initially entangled coherent states with large amplitudes and ensuring that the relative phase remains unmeasured. $G = (V, E)$ where two players, Alice and Bob, take turns selecting a vertex $w$ from the graph's vertex set. Initially, Alice picks $w_0$, after which Bob selects a neighbor $w_1$. The game concludes when Alice chooses $w_0$ such that no such vertex exists in $G$ that could serve as the starting point of any winning move for her. The final score is defined as the shortest path distance between $w_0$ and $w_f$ in $G$. Let $\alpha(G)$ represent the game score, with the goal for Alice to minimize and Bob to maximize it. For a given order $n$, let $d_i$ denote the number of vertices with degree $i$. This paper provides the exact value of $\alpha(G)$ when $d_0=d_{1}=...=d_{k-2}=0$ and $d_{k-1}\ge 1$ for $k\ge 2$. Furthermore, it compares $\alpha(G)$ to the graph's diameter, $\delta(G)$, proving the inequality $\alpha(G)\le \delta(G)+1$. In the specific case where $d_0=0$ and $d_1\ge 1$, the bound simplifies to $\alpha(G)\le \delta(G)$. Finally, a sufficient condition is established under which $\alpha(G)=\delta(G)+1$. This paper introduces a framework designed to address data scarcity and sparsity within a specific CS context: translanguaging, a phenomenon prevalent in South Asia where speakers fluidly alternate between Standard and Non-Standard languages within sentences. Focusing on Marathi-English translanguaging, the primary objective is to classify whether each sentence expresses empathy or lack thereof. Since empathy classification in CS remains underexplored, the initial step involves analyzing the structural and linguistic characteristics of textual data to establish a user-defined set of CS features for empathy expression. This section highlights the emergence of empathy markers in both Standard and Non-Standard languages that differ significantly in form and meaning when code-mixed. Subsequently, we evaluate several models and their variations that account for these CS features, demonstrating that incorporating features expressed in Non-Standard languages enhances classification performance. We propose that any CS classification task should integrate NLP approaches capable of handling ambiguity and linguistic variation found in real-world data, alongside methods that utilize and account for the presence of non-standard language features. Finally, we outline several potential NLP tasks relevant to CS contexts and suggest integrating insights from linguistics concerning ambiguity and variation. Addressing data scarcity and sparsity in CS contexts remains a complex challenge, as the appropriate amount and type of annotated data vary based on the specific task and the degree of variability present. To mitigate this, we demonstrate that models capable of leveraging ambiguity and non-standard variations can effectively reduce both the volume of required annotated data and variance related to CS features. Additionally, we argue that weak supervision and weak alignment techniques hold promise for automatically annotating CS datasets to support further research in this domain. The proposed dataset and code are available at https://transling.nlp.iitb.ac.in/. To the best of our knowledge, this represents one of the initial explorations of empathy expression and classification within contextual CS environments. When compared to SPICE simulations utilizing the BSIM4 transistor model, this analytical approach demonstrates high accuracy, maintaining an average error below 3% across a broad spectrum of process conditions and output loads. Utilizing intracortical recordings from monkeys, we examined the relationship between animacy (animal vs. nonanimal) clustering and layers' histological depth. Our findings reveal distinct and opposing trends in the organization of cortical layers and the depth of functional columns based on the animacy category. Specifically, the deeper layers are more enriched with animal responses, whereas the superficial layers show a predominance of nonanimal responses. This pattern reinforces the existence of a functional amodal core dedicated to processing the semantic properties of visual stimuli. Finally, the observed association between the separation of response categories and the presence of R2 cells in deeper layers provides a functional role for these cells, which were previously considered orphans. In summary, the association between the vertical organization of response categories and the histological and functional layer-based architecture of the cortex offers an alternative perspective on the functional architecture of the ventral temporal cortex. The primary objective is to develop a robust, decentralized control framework for a fleet of robots, ensuring they maintain specific inter-robot distances and avoid obstacles, including one another. Initially, we construct a high-fidelity simulation environment based on the Gazebo robotics simulator to ensure realistic testing conditions. Subsequently, we implement a Voxel-based Reinforcement Learning (VoXL) approach, which offers faster training speeds compared to full-fidelity simulation. To address communication challenges, the paper examines two distinct methods, evaluating their performance regarding the maintenance of desired inter-robot distances and their impact from realistic latency and bandwidth constraints. Finally, the proposed approach is validated through physical experiments using a real-world robot platform. These experiments demonstrate that the learned controller's performance remains consistent between high-fidelity and low-fidelity simulations, confirming that learning can effectively bridge model discrepancies in complex, dynamic environments. Additionally, experimental results show that the learned controller surpasses model-predictive controllers in achieving desired inter-robot distances in experimental settings, despite requiring significantly longer training durations. Experimental outcomes also indicate that distance coordination is more sensitive to communication channel latency than to bandwidth limitations. Our findings demonstrate that a fleet of robots can successfully maintain desired separations in complex environments using short message lengths, even when the communication channels exhibit non-negligible latency. Furthermore, exploring the performance trade-offs between fully decentralized and centrally controlled strategies reveals that while centralized control yields higher performance, the learned controller performs robustly in highly decentralized scenarios. Experimental results further confirm that the level of decentralization can be adjusted by modifying communication parameters. Finally, experiments conducted with three, five, and ten robots demonstrate that the method scales effectively with increasing team size. To our knowledge, this represents one of the first efforts to integrate Voxel-based Reinforcement Learning into a real-world robotic system. of non-classicality in continuous-variable quantum systems. This study explores the binary transformation of system binary entanglement within thermal states under local Gaussian unitaries. We demonstrate that for thermal states in phase space, applying a phase space Wigner negativity distillation protocol with a CV threshold qubit scheme allows for the extraction of quantum correlation using only local Gaussian unitaries. Specifically, we find that a binary entanglement metric can be defined as zero for all such thermal states, regardless of the Wigner negativity present in their Wigner functions, even when the distillation protocol fails. Furthermore, we establish that the distillation efficiency is independent of the system's temperature and relies solely on the coupling strength between the system and the qubit. These findings offer valuable insights into measuring Wigner negativity through binary entanglement distillation schemes and have broader applications in quantum information processing. More significantly, they highlight that system-biquartic interactions can emerge from coupling two harmonic oscillators via qubit systems governed by linear quantum dynamics, despite the distillation process itself being facilitated by nonlinear interactions. In conclusion, these results clarify the relationship between Wigner negativity and binary entanglement for CV thermal states and provide valuable insights for assessing the non-classicality of quantum states. Additionally, the proposed distillation scheme offers a method to distill Wigner negativity from CV thermal states that would otherwise have non-negative Wigner functions, with potential utility in quantum information processing. Finally, the fact that system-biquartic interactions can arise despite involving only linear dynamics may offer new perspectives for generating quantum correlations. These results may also inspire further research on the connection between Wigner negativity and quantum correlation measures in quantum optics and related fields. However, current analysis methods often yield overly pessimistic results because they rely on simplified models of measurement correlations. This study examines how tensor networks can model measurements within quantum nonlocality frameworks to calculate secure key rates in discrete-variable time-bin continuous-variable QKD. Utilizing matrix product states, we demonstrate that standard analysis techniques fail to capture the full complexity of the quantum measurement process. By applying more advanced matrix product states with greater bond dimensions, we achieve improvements in key rate estimates by more than double compared to current methods across various error rate scenarios, resulting in economically viable QKD implementations. Consequently, tensor networks represent a promising tool for modeling measurement operators in quantum nonlocality frameworks, potentially enabling the simulation of complex operators with high efficiency. Consequently, we derive a compact and universal expression for the system's configuration quantum, showcasing its form invariance. This paper introduces the first comprehensive derivation of the cross section for spin-dependent boosted dark matter scattering. We demonstrate that the resulting cross section maintains a factorized structure, enabling efficient computation in both momentum and position space. Leveraging this factorization, we derive an explicit formula for the hadronic level spin-dependent scattering amplitude, which is crucial for linking model predictions to experimental data. Nevertheless, these approaches often struggle with inefficiency and a lack of transferability when dealing with large, complex distributions of expert demonstrations. To address this, recent research has introduced both model-based and generative techniques to extract the most informative data points for fitting the underlying distribution. This study demonstrates that these methods can be applied to learn both the value function and the behavioral policy directly from the original demonstration data. Our findings indicate that utilizing these techniques allows for reconstruction of a latent distribution from which expert actions are likely to be drawn, enabling interpolation between them. Furthermore, because actions are sampled from a distribution, there is an inherent exploration mechanism that facilitates discovery of new actions. Finally, experimental results across various tasks reveal that leveraging the underlying distribution yields superior performance compared to using the full set of expert actions. , this study examines the deformation of conservation laws in both elastic and inelastic particle collisions. We demonstrate that the commutativity of rapidities—which serve as parameters for Lorentz transformations—allows us to derive the Hagedorn theorem for massive particles without relying on the initial assumptions previously required. This approach also enables the calculation of the multiplicity distribution function. Furthermore, by applying the Jacobi identity to the noncommutative space-time parameters, we establish an additional constraint on the momentum transfer during inelastic collisions. Finally, we explore the implications of the noncommutativity parameter $a$ on the kinematic properties of elastic collisions, such as scattering angles and momentum distribution. The analysis indicates that both elastic and inelastic collision theorems can be considered indicators of noncommutative space-time. Additionally, the magnitude of the parameter $a$ can be estimated using the fluctuation intensity of the multiplicity distribution. This parameter is anticipated to be significant in hadronic and leptonic processes involving high-energy, high-multiplicity events. Additionally, the parameter $a$ is expected to influence the particle production mechanism within hadrons and leptons. In the context of multiplicity distributions, the findings align with the KNO scaling observed experimentally in high-energy hadron and leptonic collisions. These results are derived under the assumptions of two-body scattering kinematics and the absence of a preferred space-time direction. The scope of these findings is confined to the regime where $a^2 \ll \lambda_{c}^2$.
