However, this paper introduces an infinite one-dimensional (1D) qubit-quantum dot chain that remains robust in its topological phase despite perturbations that grow with the system's size. We demonstrate that this unconventional model can be maintained using only two local buffers. Furthermore, we utilize the position of defect states to establish topological quantum memory within the qubit-quantum dot system. Notably, this memory achieves perturbative immunity in the thermodynamic limit without necessitating additional quantum resources. These features make the one-dimensional chain an ideal candidate for implementing one-qubit operations and various two-qubit gates. Furthermore, we propose a detector for bit-flip errors affecting the stored information to facilitate error correction. Finally, we examine the model's behavior under time-dependent interactions to explore its potential for error mitigation. In summary, the one-dimensional qubit-quantum dot chain offers a pathway to store and protect both classical and quantum information against increasing environmental perturbations as the system scales up. This capability is vital for the reliable operation of topological quantum computing architectures. Additionally, the model provides heuristic insights into the emergence of boundary modes in higher-dimensional topological systems. These findings suggest that the proposed one-dimensional chain can serve as a foundational component for constructing topological quantum devices. (More details can be found at arXiv:2003.01230) [1]. While quantization has long been the standard method for compression, it typically compromises accuracy. This paper introduces a novel approach, Quantization-Aware Training (QAT), designed to mitigate compaction-induced accuracy loss a priori, thereby maintaining the model's performance in downstream tasks more effectively than quantization alone. To further preserve accuracy, we develop an adaptive quantization algorithm that dynamically adjusts bit-widths based on the sensitivity of specific layers and the confidence levels of individual neurons. This technique maximizes the compression ratio while maintaining accuracy, even in the high-accuracy regime where simple quantization methods fail. Experimental results demonstrate that our QAT-trained model achieves the same accuracy with 30% fewer bits compared to the original model when using quantization alone, and it outperforms other QAT-based compression techniques. Consequently, this approach enables the training of dialogue models with ultra-low bit counts for lightweight mobile applications. This paper introduces a novel framework that leverages the psychological principles of chunking and schema to enhance explainability through three core tenets: (1) knowledge is organized through schemas; (2) comprehension relies on schema activation; and (3) learning involves schema acquisition. We demonstrate that this philosophical foundation yields three novel criteria for AI explainability, which we applied to evaluate three leading explainable AI (XAI) techniques. Our findings indicate that current methods fall short of these new criteria, and we outline future research directions aimed at developing AI models that satisfy these requirements. By adhering to this philosophy, we aim to create a trustworthy ecosystem where users can foster collaborative knowledge through schemas, derive knowledge from data streams, and ensure that AI systems remain transparent and understandable. This approach offers hope for a future free of black-box algorithms, where algorithmic knowledge is shared between humans and machines. The proposed philosophy and schema-based explainability criteria offer new avenues for researchers and practitioners to develop trustworthy AI systems. We hope this work will inspire further investigation into the intersection of AI and human psychology. interest in developing a Quantum Machine Learning (QML) framework that integrates quantum algorithms with machine learning models. This paper examines a specific subclass of quantum circuits within a QML framework, proposing an algorithm designed to identify the parameters of these circuits. We analyze the likelihood function associated with the circuit, derive the corresponding gradient descent updates, and establish an error bound for the resulting parameter estimation algorithm. This methodology is particularly valuable for quantum-enhanced machine learning applications, addressing the critical challenge of characterizing or verifying quantum circuits that provide a potential quantum advantage. As a demonstration, we apply our estimation technique to a Parity quantum circuit, a well-known example in Quantum PCA studies, which aims to distinguish two classes of data points by encoding information into the relative phases of the final quantum state. Our findings demonstrate that this estimation method can efficiently and accurately recover the parameters of such circuits. Additionally, we develop a procedure to identify the set of classes within the circuit's parameter space that best fit a provided training dataset. We conclude by outlining how this approach can be extended to more complex circuits, such as Variational Quantum Eigensolvers and Quantum Kernel machines. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundation for utilizing information processing capabilities that surpass the limits of purely classical methods. Furthermore, it serves as a viable strategy for maximizing the performance of near-term quantum devices by optimizing the parameters of parameterized quantum circuits. All simulations were conducted using the Qiskit and Cirq software development kits. The orbital angular momentum arises from the recoil of energetic vacuum photons and scales as $n^2$, increasing more rapidly than the $-2n\hbar$ kinetic angular momentum associated with the Landau states. Consequently, the total angular momentum becomes unbounded below. To address this instability, we propose a theoretical framework involving anomalous electromagnetic couments for charged particles within magnetic fields. This proposal, which relies on a non-linear interaction between electromagnetic photons and charged particles, is supported by the quest for mathematical consistency and empirical evidence from non-linear QED in strong magnetic fields. We demonstrate that the anomalous coupling successfully stabilizes the system against vacuum instability. Finally, we analyze the resulting non-linear electromagnetic equations and their connection to the Euler Heisenberg equation. Furthermore, we explore potential constraints on this anomalous coupling derived from observations of pulsars with extremely strong magnetic fields. We find that experimental data align with the theoretical prediction that the electromagnetic vacuum behaves non-linearly in the presence of strong magnetic fields. This conclusion is strongly reinforced by the observation of magnetic starquakes in highly active pulsars. Consequently, we argue that this non-linear behavior of the electromagnetic vacuum constitutes one of the most significant achievements in modern physics. We also discuss the broader implications of this argument regarding the anomalous coupling of electromagnetic photons to the Higgs field, which may offer an explanation for the smallness of the Higgs mass. While balancing strategies that uniformly distribute workload across all servers are typically designed to lower energy usage and enhance performance, they suffer from excessive overhead and fail to leverage the heterogeneity of modern server fleets. We introduce a novel load balancing approach called the Disjoint Chunked scheme, which eliminates the overhead associated with traditional uniform distribution and capitalizes on server heterogeneity by dividing the server population into distinct chunks, each employing its own load balancing mechanism. This work provides a detailed performance and energy analysis of cloud environments utilizing this scheme. Furthermore, we conducted extensive simulations to evaluate and compare the scheme's performance and energy efficiency against two existing methods: (1) Equal Chunked distribution and (2) All-to-All distribution. Our detailed analysis and simulation results demonstrate that the Disjoint Chunked scheme achieves superior performance and energy efficiency compared to uniform distribution and are robust across various cloud scenarios. We also present a real-world performance study of the Disjoint Chunked scheme. Finally, we conclude by proposing a method to automatically determine the optimal number of chunks based on specific cloud scenarios. The source code for the Disjoint Chunked scheme is available at: https://github.com/DisjointChunked/load_balancing_scheme. We establish a polynomial-time algorithm for deciding this game and demonstrate that it is capable of distinguishing polynomial-size circuits with a polynomial degree between classical and quantum models. Furthermore, we analyze several notable nonlocal games, including those associated with the Clifford circuit, shadow oracle, and Clifford+T circuits, all of which can be resolved using this algorithm. These findings significantly expand the range of nonlocal games with reduced complexity and offer an improved algorithm for determining the Clifford+T game. Additionally, our work provides the first polynomial-time algorithm, applicable to quantum computers, for the shadow oracle game. By leveraging this algorithm, we also derive several related findings. Notably, we show that determining shadow oracle games remains NP-hard even when restricted to games with two measurements. Moreover, we investigate various approximation versions of shadow oracle, proving that finding approximations with an approximation ratio of $1/2 + \epsilon$ (where $\epsilon > 0$) is impossible in polynomial time for both quantum and classical computers. However, we observe that finding an approximation for the same ratio in the Clifford+T game is feasible using a polynomial-time quantum algorithm. These results offer deeper insights into the complexity of these nonlocal games and their approximation factors. Finally, our work presents the strongest connection identified to date between the shadow oracle and Clifford+T games, while also identifying other related complexity relationships. More significantly, by considering a single-player variant of shadow oracle, we construct a quantum depth hierarchy for Clifford circuits, which effectively differentiates quantum circuit depths with varying complexities. This hierarchy offers an alternative to the Bravyi method, while also providing both nonlocal and local approaches to distinguish circuit depths. Our research holds substantial value for investigating the complexity of Clifford circuits and the shadow oracle. Additionally, the study of shadow oracle reveals new light on the relationship with local Clifford circuits, potentially deepening understanding in this area. Regarding the single-player variant of shadow oracle, we develop an algorithm to decide it and use this to differentiate linear-depth Clifford circuits from those with greater depth. This offers an alternative to the Bravyi approach for distinguishing linear-depth Clifford circuits. Overall, this paper presents multiple significant contributions to the field of nonlocal games. By introducing the single-player variant of shadow oracle, we decide its complexity and employ it to distinguish between linear-depth Clifford circuits and Clifford circuits of higher depth. Our work distinguishes itself from the Bravyi approach by providing both nonlocal and local methods

This pattern is also evident in the fundamental and higher-order acoustic modes of astrophysical pulsations. We further explore this notion by proposing a theoretical framework where dark matter and baryonic matter are treated as distinct fluid components within a single cosmic fluid. In this model, the fundamental pulsation of the dark matter fluid is an integer multiple of the pulsation of the baryonic fluid, which is driven by the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) signal. Furthermore, we have investigated the concept of "almost-integers" across various fields, including general relativity, quantum mechanics, and biology, and will continue to expand its application in future research. Our model accounts for the dual nature of entrainment as both a control variable and a control mechanism within dialogue systems. To demonstrate this efficacy, the paper includes a simulation study utilizing a speech production and perception model. This study explores various control parameters and illustrates how the system can enforce alignment on a listener, even when the listener is a natural language processing model. The proposed methodology provides a framework for computational models to represent and control the phenomenon of conversational alignment. \section{Introduction}
Action segmentation is a fundamental component of vision-based human action recognition, aiming to label every frame in a video with a class label and corresponding start and end timestamps. While this task is essential for numerous applications, the overwhelming number of action classes and the requirement for precise temporal annotations make large-scale dataset curation a significant challenge. Conventional approaches typically rely on a small collection of publicly available datasets, each containing only a few hundred videos and a limited set of action categories. Consequently, researchers are often restricted to recognizing actions from a narrow subset of a broader taxonomy rather than a wide range of categories. Moreover, achieving satisfactory performance on existing benchmarks typically demands hundreds of hours of manual annotation.

This paper demonstrates the potential of self-supervised deep networks to generate accurate labels for such datasets, thereby reducing the annotation burden to less than 10%. By employing a novel graph-based self-supervision technique, we can accurately segment both actions and objects within hundreds of hours of video data curated from hundreds of existing datasets, all while maintaining less than 5\% manual annotation. Our approach is designed to be easily extensible to other video or image recognition tasks. However, if the target dataset contains labels from the source training dataset that are incorrect due to distribution shifts, minimizing this distance can cause the model to learn inaccurate label mappings. Consequently, numerous domain adaptation approaches are unable to cope with such shifts because they fail to prevent the model from learning wrong mappings. By doing so, ADF3 helps eliminate the negative impact of label mismatches in the target dataset, as these mismatches do not affect the source domain training data. This study introduces a novel method to create gridless and grid-based precomputed atmospheric models by leveraging the outputs of a prior computation. We apply this technique to T-DUST, a grid-based code that simulates blackbody radiation modified by molecular absorption and dust opacity. The methodology is also adaptable for grids of solar-composition atmospheres and planetary models. By evaluating a reduced set of precomputed models against a much larger set of on-the-fly computed models, we demonstrate that the former can effectively approximate the latter. Specifically, for T-DUST, we show that utilizing a library of only 3,000 and at most 10,000 models is sufficient to represent 30,000 on-the-fly models with an average flux error of less than 0.01% and a maximum error of 0.1%. Furthermore, we present a method to estimate the expected flux error for any given model based on the T-DUST code due to the inclusion of precomputed models. Our results indicate that grid-based models require a higher number of precomputed models to achieve accurate representations compared to gridless models. For T-DUST, we find that 100,000 grid locations necessitate at least 300,000 models, whereas gridless models can be accurately approximated by as few as 10,000. In both scenarios, the number of precomputed models can be significantly reduced by applying a weighted average to the fluxes of the constituent models. Finally, we outline a strategy for determining the minimum number of precomputed models required for a T-DUST model to ensure an average flux error below a user-defined threshold. We demonstrate that even with a limited number of LDOS moments, one can achieve highly accurate estimates of total density of states (TDOS)-based metrics, such as the magnetic anomaly index for Hund's cases (MAI). Furthermore, we calculate higher-order LDOS moments for both nonmagnetic and magnetically ordered configurations in the half-filled Mott insulator LaCuInO$_4$. By analyzing the ratio of the second to the first moment, we conclude that the MAI can be effectively represented by just two moments. This suggests that the MAI is governed primarily by the energy widths of the $3d$ band orbitals near the Fermi level. Additionally, the observed ratio aligns with empirical values derived from our first-principles total energy calculations, which indicate that electronic correlations are stronger for $3d$ orbitals with lower symmetry. For the latter, the MAI is determined exclusively by the zeroth and first LDOS moments, yielding exact results for MAI-based models and a quantitatively accurate approximation otherwise. These findings may prove valuable for the efficient computation and physical understanding of electronic strongly correlated states and their symmetries. This work constitutes the first part of a series; the subsequent part will present our general formulas for the moment-based MAI and apply them to various other systems. This presentation focuses on the application of a specific method known as "causal representation learning" to supersymmetry search events. By learning hidden causal latent variables and their observed effects from data, causal representation learning offers a more interpretable alternative to standard machine learning approaches. This additional interpretability is crucial for ensuring that data from anticipated supersymmetry search events aligns with the underlying physical model's assumptions. Utilizing simulated CMS data for a supersymmetry search targeting gluino and gluino decay into a light neutralino and jet, we constructed a generative causal representation learning model to estimate the latent structure and parameters of the data. We demonstrate how this causal framework enhances the discrimination between signal and background compared to conventional machine learning methods. Furthermore, we show that the parameters and latent variables offer a more intuitive description of the data than the raw inputs. Ultimately, we argue that causal representation learning serves as a valuable tool for analyzing supersymmetry data, facilitating the detection of deviations from the expected supersymmetry model. established a novel dataset to benchmark state-of-the-art methods for solving a classic problem: identifying duplicates within a collection of images. This paper introduces TIIS (Two-Step Image Similarity), a model that sets new state-of-the-art records on this dataset. Specifically, it operates under the assumption that two images share a common underlying representation if they exhibit similar pattern-based hashes and demonstrate high similarity in at least one of two pretrained feature models. We analyze the scenarios involving both instantaneous and accumulated interactions with the boundary. We examine three distinct scenarios: confined quarks, perturbative quark-gluon plasma, and the color-magnetic field arising from the condensation of the axial-vector meson within the QCD vacuum. Our analysis reveals that the zero-temperature equation of state for confined quarks and quark-doublet condensation aligns with nuclear matter equation of state at a magnetic field strength of $B = 10^{18}$ G. Furthermore, the zero-temperature bag constant in the quark-jet model corresponds closely to the QCD zero-temperature bag parameter. We also demonstrate that the zero-temperature equation of state for the quark-doublet condensation model matches that of nuclear matter, thereby supporting the interpretation of the QCD vacuum as a color-magnetic condensate in zero-temperature nuclear matter under strong magnetic fields. Additionally, we find that the quark jet index in the confined quark model aligns with observed jets from heavy-ion collisions, whereas the quark jet index in the quark-doublet condensation model exceeds that of the perturbative quark-jet model, providing the most stringent constraint on the quark jet index in strong magnetic fields. We demonstrate that the magnetic field dependence of the quark jet index in the confined quark model agrees with jets from heavy-ion collisions, while the perturbative quark-jet model yields a lower fit. We conclude that the quark jet index in the confined quark model can be applied to jets in quarkonium condensation within a strong magnetic field. Finally, we show that the magnetic field dependence of the quark jet index in the quark-doublet condensation model is consistent with the jets observed in the ultra-strong magnetic field of a pulsar. These findings suggest that the QCD zero-temperature bag parameter in the quark-doublet condensation model can be used to analyze the jets in the pulsar's magnetic field. In summary, we conclude that the quark jet index in the confined quark model and the QCD zero-temperature bag parameter in the quark-doublet condensation model are applicable to nuclear matter in strong magnetic fields. This work appears in Physics of Atomic Nuclei, Vol. 24, No. 1, 2022, pp. 1–10. The article is available online at http://www.phat-atom.ru/eng/2022/24/1/10/.

in federated neural network training, where sensitive user data risks exposure through the transmitted parameter updates. To address this, various techniques have been developed to either lower the information leakage or compress the update messages. However, most existing solutions lack efficiency in high-throughput communication environments, often failing to provide guarantees regarding communication cost, computational load, or communication efficiency. We present a comprehensive analysis of these methods by applying information-theoretic metrics to measure communication compression and calculating the maximum achievable communication efficiency based on given leakage and cost constraints. Additionally, we investigate the impact of imbalanced channel noise on communication efficiency. Our analysis yields two key insights: (1) When channel noise is sufficiently strong and symmetric, gradient masking and communication compression strategies yield equivalent communication efficiency; otherwise, they may produce different results. (2) For channel-masked federated learning, increasing communication rounds does not necessarily enhance communication efficiency once the channel exhibits non-IID noise characteristics. The proposed analysis metrics facilitate the comparison of communication compression techniques under specific leakage and cost limits. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods through extensive numerical experiments. The code is accessible at https://github.com/zhengruifeng/federated-learning-analysis. This instrument offers spectral coverage and resolution comparable to the space-based Herschel Interactive Exoplanet Spectrograph (HST). Utilizing a 1.3m telescope, FUSE-N achieved a resolution of R = 300 across the 150–320 nm range with an integration time of 1800 seconds, resulting in a final on-source integration of 900 seconds. The observed spectrum exhibits an overall continuum shape similar to that of the giant carbon star WISE 08543-7120 and includes prominent lines characteristic of both molecular and atomic carbon, such as C II, C III, C IV, CN, C2, and CO. Notably, IRC+10216 displays a significantly flatter continuum in the FUV region, which we attribute to dust absorption and scattering. By fitting the observed spectrum with a grid of 1D stellar atmosphere models, we determined the physical properties of IRC+10216: a mass of 5.3 solar masses, a wind velocity of 0.2 km/s, and a mass loss rate of 4.0 x 10^-5 solar masses per year. Furthermore, we conducted 3D radiative transfer calculations along a line of sight intersecting the circumstellar medium of IRC+10216, successfully reproducing the observed spectral features. These results indicate that the dust shell surrounding IRC+10216 has a scale height of approximately 1017 cm. Finally, we have compiled an inventory of dust species and dust-related molecular species within the circumstellar environment of IRC+10216. This study serves as a case study for applying the newly launched FUSE-N instrument in astrophysical research. Additionally, we anticipate that FUSE-N will enable the study of a broader array of astrophysical targets, providing high-resolution, high-quality spectra that can drive significant scientific advancements. Theory 2017], in which agents at level $n$ maximize expected utility assuming that all $m < n$ level agents play weakly rational strategies, while those at $m$ play rationalizable strategies. We demonstrate that whether the CH hierarchy converges to rationality is determined solely by the speed of payoff convergence and the rate of decay in the agents' level distribution, rendering it independent of the specific payoffs and the agents' prior rationality. Specifically, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for convergence to rationality given a fixed payoff sequence and a fixed time horizon, as well as given a fixed payoff matrix and an infinite time horizon. Furthermore, when the payoff sequence is bounded and the decay in hierarchy level is sufficiently rapid, we prove that agents' expected payoffs converge to the rationalizable payoff average. For the infinite horizon case, if the payoff sequences for both hierarchical and rationalizable agents are bounded, their respective average payoffs converge to the rationalizable payoff average. Finally, we show that if every bounded payoff sequence over CH strategies (which converge to rationality) yields payoffs no greater than those of any unbounded sequence, then every unbounded sequence must converge to the rationalizable limit. This finding serves as a generalization of the folk theorem, as it relies exclusively on the payoff matrix without requiring a specific CH sequence. We also examine a generalized folk theorem for dynamic CH, extending it to infinite horizons. In this context, we characterize the necessary and sufficient conditions on payoff matrices such that, for any CH agent sequence, agents' payoffs converge to the rationalizable payoff average. We demonstrate that for $N$-player games, a sufficient condition is the existence of $\epsilon$-rationalizable strategies that are $\epsilon$-rationalizable for every $\epsilon > 0$. For the case of two players, a sufficient condition is the existence of rationalizable strategies for every $\epsilon > 0$. In both scenarios, we present counterexamples where rationality does not emerge, indicating that these conditions are not necessarily necessary. Furthermore, for two-player zero-sum games, we prove that rationality always emerges. For general two-player games, we show that either rationality emerges or the rationalizable payoff set forms a line segment. ulating policies concerning land use, water and energy consumption, food availability, and green space planning. However, political instability and conflicts often disrupt census data collection, necessitating alternative methods to track population growth and project future needs. Utilizing remote sensing data to monitor changes in built-up areas offers a viable solution for generating reliable population-adjusted metrics. This study employs 30-meter resolution Landsat 8 images from 2018 and 2019 to assess the feasibility of detecting population change in South Sudan, a country where a prolonged civil war hindered the 2017 census. We extracted built-up areas from the 2018 image through unsupervised classification and supervised object-based change detection using a sample built-up area from the 2019 image. The analysis reveals a significant increase in built-up land between 2018 and 2019, with an annual growth rate of 10.82% and a 2018 base of 2,282 hectares. The study area expanded from 21,522 hectares in 2018 to 25,805 hectares in 2019, with the non-built-up portion shrinking from 19,240 hectares to 15,523 hectares. This 19.3% reduction in non-built-up land aligns with the United Nations Population Division's estimate of an 18.9% population increase in South Sudan during the 2018–2019 period. The strong correlation between population growth and built-up land expansion suggests that remote sensing of built-up areas serves as an effective tool for estimating population dynamics in regions where censuses are unfeasible. Furthermore, the rapid increase in built-up land indicates the necessity for sustainable urbanization policies and infrastructure development to support future population needs. The successful application of Landsat 8 images for this purpose opens new avenues for utilizing lower-resolution satellite data in similar contexts within South Sudan and other conflict-affected areas. Additionally, this research can be extended to longer time periods to facilitate the long-term monitoring and modeling of population growth using multi-temporal remote sensing data. Finally, the methodology developed in this study can be adapted for other regions to assist in formulating policies and infrastructure plans capable of accommodating future population demands. Furthermore, this work contributes to the growing field of leveraging machine learning and artificial intelligence to transform geospatial data into valuable information. As a proof

on developing a comprehensive theory for the thermodynamics of non-equilibrium systems. This framework relies on two core equations: the non-equilibrium entropy production and the non-equilibrium potential. Recently, these principles have been extended to active matter systems, yielding new analytical results for active matter dynamics. However, this overview demonstrates the limitations of applying entropy production as a universal minimization principle across all time scales. Specifically, while the variational approach effectively predicts the quasiastatic behavior of active matter, it fails at time scales where the system's non-equilibrium steady state is not yet fully established. Consequently, an explicit minimization principle valid only in the immediate vicinity of active equilibrium is proposed. The utility of this method is demonstrated through two significant applications: a refined analysis of the active gel's response to shear deformation and an investigation into the quasicstatic compression of an active particle within a time-dependent external potential. These findings indicate that variational methods remain valuable for analyzing active matter in newly identified scenarios. Furthermore, the paper establishes a conceptual distinction between active matter compression and the classic problem of the particle in a box, clarifying the origin of active matter's exceptional escape probability from confinement. The study also references the author's 2019 review, [arXiv:1910.01827], for additional context and previous applications of both entropy production and variational principles in active matter. Key terms include thermodynamics, active matter, variational principle, entropy production, active particle, and active particle escape. PACS numbers are 05.40.-a, 05.70.Ln, and 87.16. 05.

We introduce a method for simulating the dynamics of active particles confined within a time-dependent potential, leveraging recent analytical findings regarding their escape probability. Our approach employs a time-dependent effective potential capable of reproducing the correct escape dynamics, alongside a time-dependent chemical potential that acts as a source term in the hydrodynamics of the system's density. This proposed method proves effective in describing the escape process of an active particle trapped by a harmonic potential, yielding accurate results even with a minimal number of simulation particles across both two and three dimensions. Key words: active matter, active particle escape, effective potential, effective chemical potential, simulation. PACS numbers: 05.40.-a, 05.70.Ln, 87.16. PDC. olecule conversion within spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensates, with a specific focus on the impact of spin mixing angle anisotropy and magnetic field orientation. A key finding is that the circular polarization state can be achieved by aligning the magnetic field perpendicular to the spin mixing vector. Furthermore, we present a scheme for generating spin-squeezed states that accounts for both angle anisotropy and field orientation, which relies on the coherent Raman process involving virtual off-diagonal spin states. This is supported by experimental data indicating that angle anisotropy significantly diminishes the degree of spin-squeezing. Additionally, we explore how magnetic field orientation influences the efficiency of the coherent atom-molecule conversion process. Our analysis, conducted through both the Hamiltonian and the Tanaka-Fujii order parameter, reveals that optimal molecular generation occurs when the magnetic field is parallel to the spin mixing direction. However, in this specific orientation, we find that the spin-squeezed state becomes impossible to achieve. These findings offer a viable approach for simultaneously generating both spin-squeezed states and molecules. Finally, we discuss how accounting for angle anisotropy refines the predictions of the nonclassical region in the Jammin-Parkins-Cummings parameter space. These results hold potential for developing advanced quantum metrology and for deepening the understanding of strongly interacting many-body systems. Although a single Bayesian structure can often solve both, we distinctively apply a joint Bayesian approach to one and a sequential empirical Bayesian approach to the other. This decision is driven by the fact that solving both problems simultaneously is as expensive as the joint method, whereas empirical Bayesian techniques offer significant efficiency gains when applied separately. Our analysis demonstrates that the sequential empirical Bayesian method is competitive with the joint Bayesian method for the polynomial chaos expansion inverse problem, provided hyperparameters are selected appropriately. Furthermore, by extending the sequential framework—where only a single hyperparameter needs estimation—to higher-dimensional problems, we show that this approach, when paired with a uniform prior, significantly outperforms the standard joint empirical Bayesian method. These results highlight that hyperparameter estimation is critical to the joint empirical Bayesian method's failure in this context. Consequently, we conclude that sequential empirical Bayesian methods are superior for solving high-dimensional inverse problems. The paper also includes a review and comparison of different Bayesian strategies and presents a general recommendation on when and how to use the sequential approach. Finally, we discuss future potential improvements and enhancements to both statistical methods. Our findings are based on two benchmark inverse problems from the literature: the Lorenz system and the 2D Navier-Stokes equation. For the Lorenz inverse problem, we evaluate the sequential empirical Bayesian method's performance across various prior distributions and different numbers of training data points. We demonstrate that this approach is competitive with the joint Bayesian method when the joint posterior is challenging to sample from and when appropriate prior distributions are selected. Additionally, we illustrate that the sequential empirical Bayesian method outperforms the joint approach if these priors are not specifically tailored. Regarding the 2D Navier-Stokes inverse problem, we compare the sequential empirical Bayesian method against both the joint empirical Bayesian method and a new joint full Bayesian approach, which incorporates the stochastic Kansa method for Bayesian polynomial chaos sampling. The sequential empirical Bayesian method proves competitive with the joint full Bayesian method, with results highly dependent on the number of training data points. Moreover, we find that the joint full Bayesian method outperforms the sequential empirical Bayesian method if training data points are limited to 1000. We also examine the impact of different sampling strategies on the sequential empirical Bayesian method's performance. Finally, we establish that this sampling strategy is competitive with joint methods provided that prior distributions are carefully chosen. We further demonstrate that the sequential empirical Bayesian method is competitive with the joint full Bayesian method

a social deduction board game where players divide into two opposing factions to eliminate one another. This study examines the game through the lens of \textit{Boolean network theory}, a mathematical framework developed to model complex systems. In this context, individual players function as agents within a complex network, with interactions occurring via simple boolean rules. A critical aspect of this theory involves characterizing the network's complexity using the fragmentation (or bifurcation) diagram of the agent interaction map. We demonstrate that the Mafia game network possesses a high degree of complexity, though it undergoes a bifurcation that lowers this complexity compared to other network models. Furthermore, analysis of the Mafia network's maximum path length indicates that the gameplay involves both local and global interactions. Finally, we show that the complexity of the Mafia network rises as the total number of players decreases. Additionally, we introduce a new analysis method grounded in game symmetry to enhance the descriptive power of the Mafia network complexity. This approach is particularly effective when the player count is odd. The paper concludes with a \textit{Study on Mafia Networks}, a \textit{Survey on Mafia Game Research}, and an exploration of \textit{Future Research on Mafia Game}. As a component of this survey, we reference a \textit{Bibliography on Social Deduction Game Research}. The primary objective of this research is to propose modeling Mafia using Boolean Network Theory and to investigate the game's complex network characteristics. By understanding these characteristics, we aim to assist both existing and future players in developing countermeasures against the game's complexity, thereby creating a more balanced and enjoyable experience. We anticipate that applying this analysis method to other social deduction games will yield insightful results. To demonstrate this, we have already applied the method to the popular game Werewolf with encouraging outcomes. The authors extend their gratitude to all contributors who made this research possible. existence of a fifth giant planet in 55 Eri b's system remains uncertain. We present the outcomes of our radial velocity survey utilizing the HARPS spectrograph and the ESO E-ELT's ESPRESSO instrument, which aimed to identify additional giant planets orbiting 55 Eri b with orbital periods exceeding 1000 days. We observed 12 periods near 1000 days for both HARPS and ESPRESSO; however, statistical analysis indicated that these were driven by noise rather than genuine planetary signals. A joint analysis of the ESPRESSO data further confirmed the absence of any significant planetary signal. Consequently, we conclude that a fifth giant planet with a period greater than 1000 days orbiting 55 Eri b is unlikely. The ESPRESSO observations covered approximately 60 days of the orbital period, establishing that the system is too close to the HARPS and ESPRESSO observatories for the detection of such a planet. In summary, our results indicate that if a fifth giant planet exists around 55 Eri b, it must have an orbital period longer than 2.5 years. This study represents the initial effort to search for a co-orbital giant planet with a period surpassing 1000 days in the 55 Eri b system. The ESPRESSO observations were designed specifically for this purpose. To our knowledge, this is also the first investigation seeking evidence for a fifth giant planet with a period greater than 2.5 years around 55 Eri b. We anticipate that similar searches for co-orbital giant planets with periods exceeding 2.5 years could be conducted for other systems using the ESPRESSO instrument at the ESO E-ELT. This approach could significantly advance our understanding of planetary system formation and evolution. Finally, we have compiled a list of 12 stars that are prime candidates for hosting a co-orbital giant planet with an orbital period longer than 2.5 years. Searching for such planets using the ESPRESSO instrument would be highly valuable for understanding the formation and evolution of planetary systems. Our findings will be published in the associated data paper. (Abstract abridged)

However, the inherent sparsity of MoE is often accompanied by a high probability of dead experts who never receive any data. This issue significantly hinders parallel training, as the dynamic nature of MoE complicates task scheduling and makes performance monitoring and control more challenging. This paper introduces the CSP MoE, a novel approach designed to mitigate these challenges. Rather than dynamically selecting experts, CSP MoE employs a control strategy to systematically assign data to each expert in a cyclic pattern. Consequently, CSP MoE eliminates the need for complex tasks within the scheduler, monitoring module, and performance control units. To our knowledge, CSP MoE represents the first method that guarantees the activation of every expert during training. Experimental evaluations on the A100 GPU platform confirm that CSP MoE achieves both the reduction of computational complexity and the full utilization of all experts. Compared to SmMoE, a state-of-the-art MoE variant, CSP MoE reduces the FLOPs per parameter by 4.27 times while utilizing 23.5% fewer experts per forward pass, and it delivers superior and more stable overall performance. Additionally, CSP MoE lowers the memory overhead per expert during the scheduling process by 90% compared to SmMoE. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengqiangliu/CSPMoE. behaviors are crucial in contemporary society, driven by their scale, speed, and extensive reach. This research examines information diffusion within social networks by analyzing the adoption patterns of a specific behavior using a modified version of the Bass diffusion model. We employ a combined approach integrating machine learning and the enhanced Bass framework to evaluate the impact of various network structural metrics on the diffusion of digital (social media) and traditional word-of-mouth behavioral processes. Specifically, we investigate how network degree distribution, transitivity, and the degree of centrality of actors influencing diffusion alter diffusion rates. Our findings indicate that higher degrees of clustering and centrality within the network accelerate the diffusion rate. Additionally, we observe that degree distribution patterns, particularly power-law distributions, consistently amplify diffusion rates. Finally, we conclude that a study's focal node acts as a catalyst for diffusion; as network degree increases, diffusion velocity rises, whereas removing nodes with lower degrees causes it to decrease. This work demonstrates that network structure is integral to diffusion dynamics, implying that interventions targeting network structure can facilitate or hinder the spread of behaviors, ultimately aiding in the design of more efficient marketing strategies. This estimation, in turn, serves as the basis for calculating degree-of-freedom metrics to guide the design of detection algorithms. When this methodology is applied to both channel memory and the effective number of antennas—determined via under-sampling analysis—it aligns with the theoretical memory count defined by the minimum necessary under-sampling rate to preserve channel information, as established by the sampling theorem. Although the resulting estimator is biased, its asymptotic behavior accurately matches the target quantity, confirming its reliability as a metric for characterizing channel dynamics in unamplified optical wireless communications (OWC). This characterization is particularly pertinent for massive optical arrays, given the computational and numerical challenges associated with sampling theory in this context. Consequently, the under-sampling rate, expressed as the ratio of antenna count to channel memory, emerges as a key metric for assessing array performance in future massive optical arrays, a task complicated by the nonlinear nature of OWC and other difficult analytical issues. Consequently, over the past decade, metrics such as the effective memory factor ($\mathcal{M}$-factor) and the spatial Nyquist range have been proposed to facilitate optical MIMO design. Specifically, the $\mathcal{M}$-factor has been suggested as a proxy for channel memory. However, recent research has identified two distinct definitions for the $\mathcal{M}$-factor, leading to conflicting conclusions regarding its behavior at high power. Furthermore, the practical utility of both the spatial Nyquist range and the $\mathcal{M}$-factor remains ambiguous. This study investigates the relationship between these two metrics and evaluates their suitability as measures of nonlinear memory. The analysis begins by rigorously defining the spatial Nyquist range and demonstrating its equivalence to the $\mathcal{M}$-factor. Subsequently, a new, rigorous definition of the $\mathcal{M}$-factor is introduced to resolve existing ambiguities and confirm its consistency with the spatial Nyquist range. Finally, the validity of these metrics as practical measures of nonlinear memory is assessed through numerical analysis of discrete-time channel samples. The findings indicate that while the $\mathcal{M}$-factor remains useful in low-power scenarios, it fails as a practical metric in the highly nonlinear regimes typical of current and future optical wireless links. is frequently the primary target for malware. Although novel attack vectors are emerging, current security mechanisms on Android primarily rely on the strict sandboxing of individual applications, leaving a significant vulnerability through the exploitation of inter-application vulnerabilities (IAVs). While recent research has explored IAVs from various angles, there remains a critical gap in the systematic identification and analysis of vulnerabilities stemming specifically through IAVs. This study aims to detect vulnerabilities that enable malware to execute privileged operations by leveraging interactions with legitimate apps. By analyzing 15,000 Android apps, we developed an automated system that localizes sensitive components, maps their interaction flows, and detects potential intrusion paths. Our methodology involves a multi-stage process: first, leveraging Android's structured codebase to identify sensitive apps and components via a deep neural network; second, utilizing a long short-term memory (LSTM) model to analyze interaction flows; and third, employing a vulnerability-sensitive dependency graph to pinpoint potential intrusion paths. Furthermore, we established a feature set grounded in intrusion scenarios to enhance detection accuracy, resulting in an average accuracy improvement of 9%. Finally, we conducted extensive experiments on 15,000 apps to evaluate our system's performance, and our findings on identified issues are being submitted to the Android Security Laboratory for thorough analysis and on-device validation. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art intrusion path detection methods. We believe this system will significantly advance the understanding of IAVs and pave the way for the creation of more effective security mechanisms capable of mitigating these risks. Our simulations track the movement of solid material by integrating the Navier-Stokes equations with a set of equations governing N-body particle interactions. Our goal is to devise a robust construction phase algorithm that generates a promising initial network when all transportation requests are known. By applying this algorithm repeatedly to all possible scenarios derived from the original uncertain instance, we produce a high-quality multi-scenario network. The results demonstrate the value of this proposed method. Furthermore, these networks can serve as a foundation for developing new "design and operate" algorithms for uncertain ride-sharing problems. Finally, we emphasize that the proposed Track-and-Stop framework and its underlying algorithms are applicable to various combinatorial optimization challenges involving multiple scenarios. These include not only related ride-sharing and real-time update problems but also diverse scenarios in combinatorial optimization with uncertain parameters and multi-criteria combinatorial optimization. In these contexts, each scenario or objective can be addressed independently using existing robust construction phase algorithms to generate a initial network of promising solutions in each scenario by repeatedly applying those algorithms to all possible scenarios of the original instance. Subsequently, a coordination phase algorithm can be employed to improve these initial networks. Future research will investigate effective "design and operate" algorithms to utilize these initial networks, as well as the specific parameters governing this process. This natural conformal transformation generates an effective interaction between dark matter and the matter sector. We examine this proposed mechanism within a simple scalar-tensor model, demonstrating how the resulting effective coupling between dark matter and standard model matter can resolve discrepancies in the cosmic microwave background, nucleosynthesis, and large-scale structure. This leads to a "symmetry-protected" dark matter scenario, characterized by an exponentially suppressed interaction cross-section and enhanced stability against nuclear scattering. A model parameter, which controls the scale of symmetry breaking in the Jordan frame, can be directly linked to observable data. Consequently, this approach offers a viable framework for resolving tensions in early-universe cosmology. Such models are inherently multi-component and predict specific relationships between parameters, distinct from the simple $\Lambda$CDM model, thereby defining unique signatures in cosmological observations. Our methodology is applicable to any scalar field theory, and we outline its steps to facilitate this analysis. However, the timescales required to capture binding events and sample binding pathways and transition states often exceed the capabilities of current high-performance computers. To address this, a two-step enhanced sampling method is proposed. First, a coarse-grained model, which retains the atomistic system's characteristics but operates on a longer timescale, is used to run an umbrella sampling experiment. This generates a low-dimensional umbrella sampling coordinate system (USC) that retains the original high-dimensional system's features. Second, in the high-dimensional space, the free energy landscape is reconstructed using the previously established USC to identify binding pathways and transition states. Finally, a coordinate system that separates the binding phase from the non-binding phase is identified to facilitate the sampling of binding events. This coordinate system, termed the binding-ness coordinate system (BCS), serves as the most effective sampling coordinate to accelerate binding events. This paper introduces the methodology and its underlying theory to facilitate its application. This research details the hardware and software architecture of a successful test of a 33-unit swarm consisting of a 330-gram UAV. While recent research has concentrated on deriving CD protocols based on individual emergent AGPs, such methods often require many-body interactions that hinder practical implementation. This work introduces a novel counterdiabatic driving scheme that utilizes only one-body CD interactions, regardless of the specific AGP employed. While acoustic modeling has reached saturation, achieving human-level accuracy typically requires language modeling (LM) technologies to be advanced enough to surpass rich human transcriptions, a challenge that has remained unresolved for over a decade. This paper presents the incremental progress made over the last decade towards solving this problem. We observe that while the industry has made significant strides in LM, ASR has not yet reached the benchmark of rich human transcriptions. However, the gap is narrowing due to the adoption of neural network-based ASR and the elimination of difficult characters, suggesting that the current bottleneck lies in language modeling. Our research indicates that character difficulty in new domains is a primary driver of ASR performance, more so than the saturation of acoustic modeling or overall LM quality. Additionally, we demonstrate the viability of automatically generating difficulty-free character tables to further reduce this complexity and improve recognition rates. Finally, we argue that any effective LM technology for ASR must be out-of-vocabulary (OOV) capable to adequately handle these challenges. Through extensive experiments, we provide evidence supporting the critical importance of OOV-LMing across various use cases and use cases involving difficult characters. In conclusion, this paper outlines research directions aimed at closing the remaining performance gap between ASR and rich human transcriptions. By addressing these areas, we aim to eliminate difficult characters and enable the development of OOV-capable LM technologies to further enhance ASR performance. Furthermore, we emphasize the necessity of establishing new ASR evaluation benchmarks to accurately measure progress toward achieving human-level accuracy. Without such benchmarks, it remains difficult to quantify the specific research efforts required to eliminate the last remnants of this bottleneck. Our goal is to guide the community in addressing these challenges to ultimately achieve human-level ASR. To conclude, we express our hope that this work will inspire the community to push the boundaries of ASR technology. (See https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.00390.pdf for the full paper.) By integrating the EKKIS data with existing literature, we confirm that 2MASS belongs to a moving group characterized by a mean proper motion of 180 mas/yr and a mean age of approximately 10 Myr. We propose a binary system scenario to explain its existence as a young Be star. By combining the EKKIS data with literature values, we derive a fast rotational velocity of v sin i = 140 km/s. Furthermore, the spectral analysis reveals the presence of H2O and CO molecules alongside CO_{2} and C2H2 molecules, which aligns with the spectral characteristics of a young star. Through molecular dynamics simulations of silica at varying temperatures and densities—spanning temperatures from 2200 K to 2800 K and densities from 2.1 g/cm³ to 2.5 g/cm³—we generated data on both residual entropy and viscosity. Our results demonstrate both theoretically and numerically that viscosity ($\eta$) follows an exponential dependence on residual entropy ($S_{\rm{r}}$), expressed as $\eta \propto \exp(\alpha S_{\rm{r}})$, with the coefficient $\alpha$ determined by the entropic characteristics of the silica liquid. Our findings indicate that the silica liquid adheres to the Adam-Gibbs theory, which posits that viscosity is exponentially linked to residual entropy. Furthermore, the entropy-velocity correlation coefficient $C_{\rm{EV}}$ was calculated for each state point; it exhibits a linear connection with the logarithm of viscosity, allowing $\eta$ to be estimated via $C_{\rm{EV}}$. The analysis reveals an increase in $C_{\rm{EV}}$ as both temperature and density decrease. Finally, the study explores the implications of the $C_{\rm{EV}}$-$\eta$ correlation for the Adam-Gibbs theory, offering numerical validation for its fundamental postulates. In summary, this work establishes a numerical entropy-velocity correlation for silica liquids that can potentially serve as an alternative method for determining viscosity. Additionally, it provides numerical proof of the Adam-Gibbs theory, and our results suggest that the $C_{\rm{EV}}$-$\eta$ correlation may hold for other silica liquid states not yet numerically investigated. These outcomes may have significant implications for silica-based glass and ceramic materials. the universe is driven by extensive quantum entanglement between two massive, space-separated gaseous systems. We demonstrate that the dynamics of an isolated total system comprising these two gas entities can be effectively represented as the product of individual unitary evolution operators, analogous to the simplifying assumption of total separability in classical field equations. However, this total separability strictly holds only when the components are maximally entangled. Consequently, we propose that the universe may have originated in a state of total separability, characterized by maximal entanglement between two gas-like components, which subsequently evolved separately as unitary operators, leading to the current state of the cosmos. Based on this scenario, we derive that the total system's von Neumann entropy equals the sum of the individual entropies minus their mutual information, implying that the universe possesses negative mutual information. Furthermore, we analyze the first law of thermodynamics, showing that the change in the universe's total volume is proportional to this mutual information. This relationship offers an explanation for the observed accelerated expansion of the universe. Additionally, we derive the Friedmann equations from which the Hubble constant, deceleration parameter, and luminosity distance can be calculated, aligning with current observational data. We also examine the thermodynamic properties of the two gaseous components, revealing that their temperatures are equal and significantly lower than the temperature of the combined system. Finally, we explore the relationship between quantum discord and entanglement within the two subsystems, suggesting that quantum discord may serve as a viable candidate for explaining the universe's accelerated expansion. This proposed total separability offers a solution to the black hole information paradox, indicating that black holes may not exist independently but only as part of an entangled pair. Furthermore, we derive the Einstein-Rosen bridge connecting two Schwarzschild black holes from the field equations of the total system, implying that the current universe may consist of two entangled massive gaseous systems that functioned as Einstein-Rosen bridges in the early stages, accounting for the acceleration observed today. We conclude that the universe's total volume corresponds to the area of the bridge's throat, establishing that the Einstein radius is linked to the size of the universe. These findings may offer new insights into understanding the structure and evolution of the universe. Additionally, I contend that a full derivation of the Born rule is essential, and without it, quantum predictions remain underived and unexplained. Therefore, superdeterminism does not resolve the problem of justifying the specific quantum theory we observe; instead, it merely defers it to a more fundamental level. Consequently, superdeterminism does nothing to alleviate the inherent problem of justifying the Born rule itself. Any interpretation that posits hidden variables and attempts to derive the Born rule from them faces the same challenge: it must either derive the Born rule directly from the hidden variable theory or derive that theory from something more fundamental while simultaneously deriving the Born rule from that underlying theory. In the absence of such a more fundamental theory, one cannot reasonably assume the theory will take a specific form or that the Born rule will apply. Without additional, independently motivated constraints, one cannot assume that an agent within that theory adheres to specific additional assumptions. Thus, even if an interpretation simply assumes the theory's parameters and attempts to justify the Born rule, it ends up in the same predicament as any other interpretation that fails to derive the theory from a more fundamental source. While neural networks are frequently employed to handle complex tasks, their substantial size renders them impractical for resource-limited environments. To address this, model quantization and pruning are utilized to minimize both memory usage and computational load. Quantization, in particular, offers a more effective compression solution for such applications. This study introduces a novel quantization approach termed "stepwise quantization," which better balances accuracy and compression ratios. We developed a stepwise quantization algorithm that progressively reduces model quality in discrete stages, evaluating the impact on compression rates and accuracy at each step to identify the optimal step number. Our method achieved up to a 4x compression ratio with negligible accuracy loss when applied to the MobileNetV2 model across 3-bit, 4-bit, and 5-bit bit-widths. Furthermore, we demonstrated that combining stepwise quantization with model pruning yields superior compression and computational efficiency compared to using either technique independently. Finally, we provided a comprehensive analysis of the impact of stepwise quantization on inference latency. Through experiments on various datasets using MobileNetV2, our method outperformed existing quantization techniques in both compression ratios and accuracy achieved. By offering these detailed analyses, we aim to facilitate the development of more efficient stepwise quantization models in future research. This research offers valuable insights for engineers and scientists working on low-inertia power systems with coupled areas, aiming to facilitate more accurate and computationally efficient simulations. In certain kinematical regimes at high energies, the saturation momentum serves as the sole relevant scale for physical processes. Consequently, various observables demonstrate geometric scaling within these regimes. Geometric scaling represents a distinct and novel phenomenon in hadronic and nuclear physics, characterized by its simplicity and universality across different reactions and datasets. Furthermore, geometrical scaling holds significant importance for analyzing future electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions at the EIC and for studying ultra-relativistic heavy ion collisions at the LHC and RHIC. In this article, we present evidence supporting geometrical scaling from a wide array of deep inelastic scattering data, utilizing various analyses and methods. We also provide support for geometrical scaling from heavy ion collision data using various approaches. Most notably, we demonstrate geometrical scaling from the nuclear modification factor $R_{AA}$, which describes the suppression of high-$p_T$ hadrons in nucleus-nucleus collisions. We conclude by discussing several future prospects for demonstrating geometrical scaling at the EIC. Specifically, we propose measuring the saturation contribution to the nuclear modification factor $R_{pA}$ at the EIC to establish geometrical scaling in high-energy hadron-nucleus collisions. We also propose measuring the saturation contribution to the nuclear modification factor $R_{AA}$ at the LHC to establish geometrical scaling in high-$p_T$ hadron production at ultra-relativistic heavy ion collisions. Ultimately, demonstrating geometrical scaling at the EIC and the ultra-relativistic heavy ion collisions at the LHC will provide strong evidence for the saturation of the gluon distribution at high energies and for the non-linear evolution equations of QCD. We identify distinct magnetorotonal peaks and analyze their qualitative dependence on the fractional filling factor $\nu$ and the particle-to-particle interaction strength. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these modes exhibit a quadratic dispersion relation at low energies and momenta, consistent with their identification as emergent collective modes in the limit of large particle numbers. Finally, we contrast our findings regarding the nature of these excitations in both bosonic and fermionic systems. The results presented here indicate that magnetorotons serve as a universal characteristic of all quantum Hall fluids. Additionally, we suggest a potential algorithm to calculate the half-integer values of $\nu$ corresponding to this phenomenon. This work contributes to the broader understanding of fractional quantum Hall states and their theoretical descriptions. Specifically, the detailed properties of magnetorotons in fermionic systems, including the impact of particle-particle interactions, are addressed here for the first time. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the formation of magnetorotons and the emergence of quantum Hall fluids. These aspects remain unaddressed in previous studies regarding charge-neutral excitations in this system. To facilitate future research, we also include a comparison between theoretical and numerical estimates of the Berry curvature, a key factor in determining the nature of emergent quantum Hall fluids. Extensive numerical and graphical data are provided to support these conclusions. To ensure reproducibility, all figures are referenced using a system based on the caption page. We anticipate that the detailed presentation and discussion of charge-neutral excitations in both bosonic and fermionic fractional quantum Hall fluids will significantly benefit the quantum Hall community. We propose that this comprehensive treatment of magnetorotons as emergent features of quantum Hall fluids constitutes a novel and important contribution to the field. Additionally, we include a discussion of the Haldane gap as an alternative explanation for fractional quantum Hall emergence, comparing it with the magnetorotronic explanation. We demonstrate that the magnetorotronic approach offers a more intuitive and comprehensive explanation for the emergence of emergent quantum Hall fluids. However, a significant drawback of current methods is the excessive number of measurements required to accurately characterize a quantum process, a limitation known as the "measurement problem." A prominent strategy to address this involves exploiting known prior information about the process, such as unitary or Clifford processes. We introduce a new, nearly optimal quantum process tomography protocol specifically for unitary and multi-step Clifford processes. Additionally, we provide a generalized approach that can be extended to other quantum processes. This method utilizes a novel quantum data-hiding technique, which was previously applied to solve the state tomography measurement problem. By employing this data-hiding method, the number of measurements needed in the laboratory is drastically reduced, depending on prior knowledge about the quantum process. Furthermore, we demonstrate a practical method to implement this data-hiding approach in multi-step Clifford processes using a Clifford circuit with a minimal width of three. Consequently, our method is directly applicable to near-term quantum devices, such as NISQ computers and quantum simulators. In summary, we present a technique that enables high-accuracy process tomography for multi-qubit Clifford processes while drastically minimizing the number of measurements required in the laboratory. These points correspond to the K and K' vertices of the Brillouin zone and represent the two underlying carbon atoms per unit cell. We demonstrate that the symmetries governing trigonal warping also apply to this two Dirac cone configuration. Consequently, established bounds on trigonal warping dictate the minimum and maximum achievable separations between the K and K' points in momentum space. A differential displacement of the K and K' points breaks time reversal symmetry. This potential reaches its maximum magnitude at the edges of the first Brillouin zone, corresponding to the K and K' locations. This surge in data necessitates a robust mechanism for storage and processing, which can be effectively achieved by integrating the IoT ecosystem with the interplanetary file system (IPFS) and Content Delivery Networks (CDNs). Specifically, the conventional method is surpassed in end-to-end delay when the system load is moderate or low. In recent years, rapidly expanding and dynamically evolving networks, particularly those in the digital and biological domains, have made it essential to monitor changes in centrality over time, alongside the development of new centrality concepts. However, existing methods for computing and comparing time-varying centrality have largely focused on geometric and topological aspects, with novel centrality definitions receiving minimal attention. This paper introduces a method for calculating and contrasting dynamic variations in a broad spectrum of centrality measures, covering both geometric and topological centrality types. These findings hold true even when considering the impact of dynamic short-term transitions on centrality identification, a factor often overlooked in previous research. Nevertheless, noise and measurement errors significantly hinder the practical implementation of VQE. To address this, we introduce a quantum-phase-Aware VQE (qAVC) designed to enhance convergence and boost computational resilience against noise by embedding problem-specific prior knowledge regarding the target state's variational phase into the ansatz. We evaluated qAVC against several existing VVE approaches using various noise models and found that incorporating phase information not only accelerates convergence but also renders the algorithm more robust against errors. Specifically, under noisy conditions, qAVC outperforms top traditional VVE methods by as much as 90% in achieving convergence. Furthermore, under noisy conditions simulating the HaH3+ molecule, qAVC reduces energy errors by up to 30% and 50% compared to other methods with the same or fewer parameters, respectively. These findings indicate that qAVC is a potent strategy for leveraging prior knowledge to optimize quantum algorithms and hold potential for practical applications in near-term quantum computing. The recent surge in deep neural networks (DNNs) has significantly advanced speech synthesis, yet most existing approaches rely on massive datasets that are difficult to acquire. This paper introduces a system designed to generate natural speech from a minimal dataset of around 100 sentences. By dynamically modeling both articulatory and acoustic features, the proposed method effectively reduces the demand for training data. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that dynamic clustering of acoustic features yields superior performance compared to mean normalization. Additionally, we demonstrate the robustness of clustering acoustically normalized acoustic coefficients across diverse speech production variations. The results validate the system's efficacy and confirm its potential for generalization to other speakers. The experimental findings indicate performance comparable to systems using 1000 sentences. The source code and executable files are available at the project website: http://www-lab.ee.t.u-tokyo.ac.jp/~kondo/Research/2016/Unsupervised_Synthesis.

We formulate an non-convex optimization problem aimed at maximizing the worst-rank transmission rate within a fair and secure framework, considering both internal interference from other users and external eavesdropping threats. The solution involves joint optimization of the base station's transmit beamformers and the RIS's phase shift configuration. To address this, we first develop an algorithm to optimize RIS phase shifts given fixed beamformer values. Subsequently, by analyzing the problem's structure, we propose an alternating optimization algorithm where beamformer design is solved using the proposed RIS optimization method. Furthermore, we illustrate the benefits of integrating RIS into the system and validate the security of the proposed beamforming strategy. We establish an explicit chain complex known as the facial complex, which serves a significant purpose in the quantum homology of a graph $Q$: when $Q$ is the commutative graph representing a non-singular algebraic variety $X$, a specific sub-complex of the facial complex is isomorphic to the de Rham complex of $X$. Furthermore, in the quantum setting, we introduce a complex termed the filtered quantum homology complex, which encapsulates the full homology of the graph $Q$. This document introduces that complex and investigates its properties. Additionally, we provide an alternative characterization of quantum homology as the homology of a specific double complex, drawing a profound analogy with Sardari's recent findings in algebraic homology. Our definition of quantum homology is motivated by its application in computing the homology of the moduli space of stable bundles on an algebraic curve. In a companion paper, we utilize the facial complex to derive a novel formula for the genus of a smooth projective curve, which generalizes a result by Daskalopoulos and Singer. This formula was initially conjectured by Sardari based on computations performed in our prior research. The current paper, however, does not rely on any findings from that conjecture. Additionally, we present examples of graphs where the quantum homology exhibits distinctly non-classical behaviors. For instance, a specific graph yields a homology group with a dimension of $20$, which is four times larger than the corresponding classical homology dimension. Conversely, in another graph, the quantum homology is more refined than the classical homology, effectively separating classes that were previously united. These examples illustrate that quantum homology is not merely an extension of classical homology but offers a homological tool of greater depth and fineness for quantum graphs. By investigating the Rindler representation of Fock states within an expanding 1+1 dimensional universe, we derive the Gelfer-Yakovlef and Band-Yakovlef images of these states. We demonstrate that the universal formula regarding the push-forward of a polynomial in the Chern classes of these bundles remains valid pointwise at the level of Chern forms. A crucial component of this proof involves the explicit calculation of the Chern curvature for the universal vector bundles with induced metrics at any point within a flag bundle. As a consequence, we derive an alternative formulation of the Jacobi-Trudi identity applicable to differential forms. Furthermore, we establish the positivity of a specific family of polynomials constructed from the Chern classes of Griffiths semipositive vector bundles. This finding offers partial validation of Griffiths' conjecture concerning positive characteristic forms, as detailed in arXiv:1605.07055. The central mechanism behind this is a polynomial inequality that connects elementary symmetric polynomials of the Chern curvature's eigenvectors; this inequality can be viewed as an algebraic version of the Maclaurin inequality and can be proven using elementary methods. Additionally, we present a comprehensive classification of positive characteristic forms on vector bundles, building on work by Ellingsrud and Strømme. Through various examples, we illustrate the distinctions and relationships between algebraic and differential characteristic forms and validate some of our findings with examples. Notably, one of our examples indicates that Griffiths semipositivity might be a necessary condition for the validity of the universal formula of Chern classes associated with characteristic forms of relative differential forms linked to projections. Finally, we investigate a specific polynomial identity related to the Chern classes of relative differential forms connected to inclusions. This identity, which serves as an important example of universality in Chern classes, was previously conjectured by the authors in [Chern classes and Segre classes of relative differential forms, Math. Res. Lett. 23 (2016), 1222-1241]. In this paper, we employ characteristic forms to provide a proof. It is worth noting that this approach offers an alternative proof for a result by Griffiths and Harris concerning the characteristic forms of tautological bundles over Grassmannians. to assign compact labels to the vertices of a graph $G$ so that the distance between any two vertices $u$ and $v$ can be deduced from their labels and a third vertex $f$ representing a failed node, provided it exist within the graph. This labeling is termed $k$-fault tolerant if, for every pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, there exists a node $f$ within a distance of $k$ from both $u$ and $v$ such that the distance $d_{G/G[f]}(u,v)$ equals the distance $d_{G}(u,v)$ minus one, where $G/G[f]$ represents the graph resulting from the removal of node $f$ and its incident edges. This work presents the first results regarding $k$-fault tolerant labeling for general graphs, offering a labeling function of size $\mathcal{O}(\log n+\log^2 k)$ for the case where $k=1$ (a previous bound was $\mathcal{O}(\log^3 n)$) and establishing an upper bound of $\mathcal{O}(\log n+\log^2 k)$ for the case where $k=\Omega(\log n)$. Additionally, graphs with an Eulerian spanning subgraph admit a labeling function of $\mathcal{O}(\log n + \log^2 k)$ for any $k$. However, the problem remains open for general graphs when $k>\log n$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the problem is NP-hard on planar graphs for fixed $k\geq 3$. Finally, we provide exact results for trees, providing labeling functions of $\mathcal{O}(\log n + \log^2 k)$ when $k$ is even and $\mathcal{O}(\log n + \log k)$ when $k$ is odd. In the latter scenario, a unique vertex $f$ exists such that $d(k,f)=k-1$, and removing $f$ results in $d_{G/G[f]}(u,v)=d_{G}(u,v)-1$ for all $u, v\in V$. This represents the first instance of an exact labeling function for $k>1$. The study also includes an analysis of the complexity of computing such labeling functions using Boolean circuits. A state-of-the-art method for capturing these similarities is the latent semantic index, achieved via semantic clustering via latent correlation (SCLC), a technique recently advanced. This study introduces a novel approach, stacked semantic clustering via latent correlation (SCLL), which utilizes the latent correlation matrix of the SCLC algorithm. SCLL integrates results from multiple independent SCLC iterations, each employing a distinct value-culling strategy. The output of SCLL is a stacked value vector; its local and global similarity properties are captured by the stacked correlation matrix (SCM).
