Furthermore, the deformation of the final nucleus alters nuclear shapes along principal axes, inducing a mixing between opposite parities. **Purpose:** To investigate these phenomena, we conducted an experiment to measure total cross sections for stable nuclei (¹⁵⁸Gd, ¹⁶⁰Gd, ¹⁶²Er, and ¹⁶⁴Er) at thermal and epithermal energies using the 4π method.
**Method:** The measurements were carried out at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Switzerland, utilizing a CeB₆ converter to generate a polarized neutron spectrum.
**Results:** The experimental data were compared against theoretical predictions based on the Hauser-Feshbach formalism, specifically the FREYA and TALYS models.
**Conclusion:** For the first time, new total cross-section data have been established for deformed nuclei. These measurements successfully demonstrate neutron capture on highly deformed nuclei across both thermal and epithermal ranges, successfully quantify the depletion of the 1/E term in ¹⁶²Er, highlight the necessity of including two-photon E2 transitions in TALYS for strongly deformed nuclei, and provide new insights into the angular momentum and parity depletion effects during capture on such nuclei. Additionally, the study offers a critical assessment of the deformation parameters employed in the TALYS model. These findings are vital for enhancing the accuracy of total cross-section calculations within the TALYS framework for neutron capture on heavy, highly deformed nuclei. **Perspectives:** This new data set will facilitate further research into low-energy neutron capture mechanisms, including direct capture on deformed nuclei, direct capture on compound nuclei, and the impact of deformation on radiative width calculations. It will also facilitate the evaluation of deformation parameters within the TALYS model. Moreover, the data will support future developments in the statistical Hauser-Feshbach model. This research was conducted to address the astrophysical objective of refining r-process nucleosynthesis calculations, which currently rely on nuclear input parameters such as neutron capture cross sections and deformations. By providing more precise capture data and deformation parameters, this study enables more accurate predictions of nucleosynthetic yields in astrophysical environments. It demonstrates that a closed-form stiction region, dependent on parameters and surrounding an invariant equilibrium set, is invariably reachable and globally attractive. The analysis reveals that asymptotic convergence is the sole outcome, necessitating at least one—and typically infinitely many—consecutive stick-slip cycles regardless of initial conditions. These theoretical findings are substantiated by numerical results featuring specific convergence examples. Consequently, the proposed approach offers a significant advancement over existing analytical and numerical methods, which often fail to characterize the frequent, repeated occurrences of stick-slip motions. As such, this framework is broadly applicable to the study of motion systems with dry friction and serves as a foundational step toward future dynamic analysis techniques. Furthermore, it will enhance the design of control strategies for motion systems that undergo repeated stick-slip behaviors. To validate the proposed method, two examples are presented. The first concerns a feedback-controlled motion system with a single actuated degree of freedom, demonstrating the typical stick-slip, localization, and stability characteristics observed in such systems. The second example involves a feedback-controlled unidirectional motion system with two degrees of freedom, highlighting its specific stick-slip characteristics and trajectory convergence. These features are analyzed using the same methodology as the first example. The results are striking and distinct from those of the initial example. Notably, a stable limit cycle is found to be unattainable for any parameter set, yet asymptotic convergence to a stick state containing exactly one slip motion is achievable. These features are generally unattainable. The findings are substantially relevant to motion systems designed to achieve rapid convergence to a target position. Finally, the key contributions are summarized. These results are significant for diverse motion systems, particularly those that repeatedly traverse a specific region where stick-slip motions are undesirable. By understanding the stick-slip characteristics and trajectory convergence, control strategies can be formulated to achieve rapid convergence to the target region without inducing repeated stick-slip motions. Additionally, these insights facilitate the development of methods to assess the robustness of motion strategies against parameter variations. It is crucial to note that the proposed methodology's effectiveness is independent of the specific stick-slip characteristics of the motion system. Therefore, the results apply to a wide range of motion systems, provided that the friction function is continuous from the right and strictly positive and lower-bounded for all velocities outside a bounded set. However, generating high-quality explanations for predicted items remains a significant challenge, as end-users often require clarification on *why* specific items are suggested to foster trust and encourage continued engagement. Consequently, this paper introduces the Explainer the Recommender model (ExplRe), designed to concurrently execute both next-item recommendation and explanation generation within a unified deep neural network. To effectively learn user-item interactions for accurate predictions, we employ Recurrent-Exclusive Gate Units (R-EXG) to capture these dynamics while simultaneously extracting features capable of articulating *why* an item is recommended. By utilizing special explainer neurons, R-ExG can formulate justifiable reasons for recommendations. We validate the model's efficacy through both quantitative and qualitative assessments across multiple real-world datasets. By applying a reduction to the non-deformed DCHE of the $D_4^{(1)}$ affine Lie algebra, we derive its first multi-soliton solution. In this process, we identify a novel elliptic equation that mirrors the structure of the wronskian solution. Subsequently, we generalize this approach to produce multi-soliton solutions for the deformed DDCHEs linked to the non-deformed DCHEs of the affine Lie algebra $\hat{sl}(2)$. For the lowest-order case, this yields the multi-soliton solutions associated with the trigonometric Crump-Hopf equation, which is mathematically equivalent to the DCHE for $\hat{sl}(2)$ at level $k=0$. Consequently, our reduction of the reducible DCHEs for affine Lie algebras offers an efficient method for constructing multi-soliton solutions for the corresponding classical Lie algebras. We anticipate that the equations and solutions presented here, along with the reduction technique, will be valuable in investigating the geometry and integrability of the Lie algebras involved. Furthermore, regarding the structure of these solutions, we observe that despite being derived from affine Lie algebras with a root system $A_1$, the solutions exhibit a $B_1$ structure in their highest-order case and a structure resembling $A_1 \oplus A_1$ in the lowest-order case. This indicates that these solutions encapsulate higher-order structures within the reducible DCHEs. Additionally, since the unreduced DCHEs for affine Lie algebras can be obtained via reductions of the reducible DCHEs for $\hat{sl}(2)$, we anticipate that the solutions for these algebras can be efficiently constructed using the same methodology. Finally, in this study, we also present the general solution for trigonometric Crump-Hopf equations. We demonstrate that these solutions are essentially elliptic Calogero-Moser type solutions with complex coupling constants, and that their structure can be derived from real coupling constant solutions. Our findings suggest that these solutions possess a higher-order structure than previously recognized. We expect that the solutions and equations for reducible DCHEs will prove useful in the broader investigation of DCHEs. Additionally, to aid in the analysis of these solutions, we have developed computer programs that successfully generate the solutions discussed in this paper

sparse vectors, such as compressed sensing, have gained traction within the statistical community. Consequently, the analysis of the asymptotic behavior of optimization algorithms on these problems is increasingly relevant. This paper examines the convergence of the optimization trajectory when solving sparse linear regression under high-dimensional and asymptotically orthogonal design conditions using a family of continuous methods. We achieve this by investigating a sequence of fluid models linked to these algorithms within a Bayesian framework. Our primary finding demonstrates that, under a weak convergence regime utilizing nonparametric estimators for population quantities, the fluid method moments closely approximate the moments of the algorithm's trajectory in a mean-square sense. We apply our main result to analyze the performance of the singular value thresholding (SVT) algorithm for low-rank matrix completion. Notably, our approach is computationally efficient and yields a closed-form solution, offering an alternative to the more commonly used alternating minimization algorithm, which has also been recently examined using a fluid method framework. Simulations indicate that SVT converges faster than alternating minimization. Leveraging our theoretical results, we demonstrate that SVT outperforms alternating minimization in terms of optimization error across various scenarios, including those where alternating minimization fails to converge to the correct solution. Our empirical findings further show that SVT remains robust to perturbations in the observations. Finally, we illustrate that the fluid method approach serves as a valuable tool for characterizing the behavior of continuous optimization algorithms in high-dimensional settings. This enables the design of algorithms with superior convergence rates and reduced error compared to established methods like SVT and alternating minimization. Specifically, we introduce a general framework for optimizing these algorithms by minimizing the divergence between the fluid method and the algorithm's trajectory, alongside its inverse. Minimizing this divergence yields performance gains over standard SVT and alternating minimization, with results validated through simulations and real-world data. Additionally, we propose estimating the divergence based on finite-sample trajectories, presenting a method that offers provable guarantees regarding the error between the finite-sample result and both the fluid method and the true objective value. Simulations confirm that this estimator effectively captures the performance of the algorithm. Through several examples, we demonstrate how these estimators can guide the selection of parameters for SVT and alternating minimization to enhance performance. Furthermore, we show that minimizing the variance of this estimator leads to improved results for SVT, surpassing the standard approach of selecting the number of iterations based on validation error. All proposed methods are scalable, requiring only a single pass over the data to estimate fluid method quantities and achieving computational complexity comparable

Additionally, we establish a connection between the classical system and its underlying quantum analogue. Universality (LFU) ratio, $R_\Sigma$, to investigate $\mu/e$ universality within the decay $B_c\to J/\psi\,\ell\nu$. This observable is especially robust against hadronic uncertainties, relying on just a single form factor. Furthermore, $R_\Sigma$ proves highly sensitive to both SM LFU violations and potential new physics contributions. We further examine its production through the $B_c$ factory mode $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ at Belle II. Our projected experimental and theoretical precision of approximately 0.5% enables a test of the SM LFU at the $10^{-4}$ level. Consequently, the $B_c$ and $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ communities are well-positioned to conduct a precise, complementary search for new physics using these $R_\Sigma$ measurements. Specifically, in $B_c$ decays, charm-scale new physics such as vector leptonic NP could induce a relative shift of several tens of percent, whereas in $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$, new vector NP effects could result in a few-percent shift. The sensitivity to SM LFU in both measurements is tested at the few-$10^{-4}$ level. The $B_c$ and $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ collaborations have established a unique synergy to probe SM LFV and non-universal LFV effects arising from vector leptonic NP. Leveraging the $R_\Sigma$ measurements, this combined sensitivity reaches approximately $10^{-4}$. We propose that the LHCb collaboration should prioritize the $B_c$ $R_\Sigma$ measurement to achieve this sensitivity. Additionally, we suggest that the $B_c$ factory community should pursue the $R_\Sigma$ search to test the $10^{-4}$ LFU sensitivity, thereby validating the combined SM LFU test capability. Furthermore, both measurements should be compared against the projected sensitivity of the $B_\mu$ measurement by the NBAL $\mu$ $E$-experiment to effectively constrain or detect vector leptonic NP. We recommend that NBAL $\mu$ $E$-communities, $B_c$ factories, and LHCb should collaborate to investigate the $B_c$ $R_\Sigma$ search using the $B_\mu$ measurement. This approach will allow for a well-determined search for vector leptonic NP with $10^{-4}$ LFU sensitivity

as networks of interconnected nodes. A central challenge in this field is determining how the architecture of a network influences the propagation of various phenomena across its structure. A prevalent method for characterizing network architecture involves analyzing the distribution of the shortest path lengths between all pairs of nodes and comparing it against the topology of a random network where every pair is connected. This comparison reveals structural properties known as structural metrics, such as the "small-world" coefficient and the typical distance coefficient. Although these metrics have been widely used, their definitions lack rigor, leading to potential misinterpretations regarding their meaning. This paper introduces a more rigorous framework for structural metrics by representing networks as probability measures on the set of shortest path lengths for all node pairs. This new definition enables a statistical interpretation of structural metrics and allows for the development of these metrics within a unified formal structure. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by applying it to various network ensembles to calculate the expected values of specific metrics. Furthermore, we apply these metrics to a biological mobility network derived from GPS data of animals, where we observe a notable correlation between the network's structure and the spatial distribution of its nodes. The proposed framework for defining and interpreting structural metrics is available at https://github.com/lorenzoferri/NetworkScienceMetrics.

eco-evolution) has gained significant traction in ecology, with its primary objective being the modeling of co-adaptive changes in ecological communities, especially among species that are closely related and capable of distinguishing one another. This paper employs the concept of finite rates of convergence to establish a rigorous mathematical framework for this area. To achieve this, a specific stochastic differential equation (SDE) model is introduced, employing the stochastic logistic framework for species dynamics while integrating major components essential for capturing finiteness, adaptation, and speciation.

Assuming a stationary regime within a multi-species community, we derive a precise mathematical representation for the stochastic logistic equation, detailing its stochastic dynamics and characteristic measures. Subsequently, utilizing rigorous probabilistic methods, we derive explicit and quantifiable conditions regarding interaction strengths and environmental stochasticity. These conditions are crucial for ensuring that species do not go extinct due to random environmental fluctuations, thereby guaranteeing the convergence of the stochastic dynamics toward multi-species coexistence. Finally, through extensive numerical simulations, we validate our theoretical findings and demonstrate that multi-species coexistence is typically robust, provided that both environmental stochasticity and speciation rates are sufficiently rapid. Furthermore, we observe that the number of coexisting species scales linearly with the speciation rate under a joint parameterization of interaction strength and environmental stochasticity. This indicates a linear increase in species richness as speciation rates accelerate, thereby elucidating a fundamental relationship between speciation and coexistence. Consequently, this reveals a core principle within the field of eco-evolutionary dynamics. Additionally, our explicit characterization facilitates a straightforward and efficient implementation of multi-species coexistence, offering a promising avenue for further exploration. Through this exploration, it is anticipated that this model will enable a deeper understanding of multi-species coexistence, thereby serving as a significant tool for the eco-evolutionary dynamics community. Through this understanding, it is also expected to contribute to broader goals concerning coevolution and multi-species coexistence. Furthermore, the explicit representation of multi-species coexistence will provide a concrete understanding of multi-species communities, acting as a practical tool for applied researchers. This practical applicability will facilitate real-world applications of multi-species coexistence, coevolution, and multi-species community dynamics. Through this practical utility, it is expected to yield tangible benefits to society regarding coevolution and multi-species community dynamics. Finally, the explicit representation will also provide a concrete understanding of multi-species coexistence, offering insights into the stability, persistence, and coexistence of multi-species communities

The analysis characterizes the probability distributions of price shifts and trading fees under different strategies, specifically investigating the impact of market manipulation techniques such as wicks and sweeps. Furthermore, the research analyzes wick interactions with multiple adjacent wicks and evaluates the viability of defensive mechanisms designed to mitigate wick attacks. The survey comprehensively reviews relevant literature and practical configurations used by AMM developers and traders, offering policy recommendations for enhancing AMM security through more robust market-making strategies and regulatory measures. Ultimately, this work aims to heighten awareness of the vulnerabilities inherent in current AMM designs within decentralized finance (DeFi) ecosystems. Furthermore, the paper derives optimal pricing functions for an risk-neutral, price-insensitive trader by solving the associated Bellman equation using closed-form solutions for both wick and standard buy/sell strategies. Finally, the study examines trading interactions between strategic agents, analyzing how different market-making strategies influence price dynamics and the distribution of price changes and fees. The authors contend that dynamic adjustment of wicks in response to market movements constitutes an effective defensive measure for developing safer AMM protocols. Additionally, the authors suggest that regulatory frameworks should mandate security standards for AMMs to prevent malicious exploits and promote transparency by requiring the disclosure of internal parameters to users. A user simulator was employed to compare trading outcomes across three distinct scenarios: a random strategy, a best-effort strategy, and an optimal strategy. The findings indicate that adopting a best-effort strategy yields profits exceeding those of a random approach by 1,268%, while the optimal strategy generates profits 287 times greater than the best-effort strategy and 3,578 times greater than a random strategy. These results underscore that strategic adaptation by market traders significantly influences the distribution of price changes and fees across multiple AMM interactions. Finally, the authors recommend that developers design AMMs with varying wick sizes to capitalize on favorable market conditions while mitigating losses in unfavorable ones. The study concludes by outlining several directions for future research. Within Bayesian models, this process is frequently conducted by generating and comparing the posterior distributions of the model's primary interests under multiple alternative specifications. To facilitate this, we introduce the sensitivity analysis package for R, which offers a diverse suite of tools designed for efficient and accessible posterior sampling, processing, and visualization. The package includes modified versions of widely used sophisticated MCMC algorithms—such as MC3, GIBBS, and SPSAM—that operate directly on the posterior distributions of the model's key interests. Our findings indicate that pathology and medical imaging models share certain concepts, which could facilitate the creation of combined multi-modal models, while also identifying future research directions. Additionally, we have released an open-source R package, "pathoRad," available at https://github.com/PathoRadR, to replicate these analyses and support further research in this area. This research was conducted in collaboration with Stanford University, the Mayo Clinic, and the University of Helsinki, with funding from the John D. and Catherine T. In this study, we introduce a generative modeling framework capable of precisely forecasting how surface termination impacts material stability across entire phase diagrams. By employing a novel energy predictor paired with a discriminator, our model forecasts the energetic consequences of surface termination and demonstrates a marked improvement over standard density functional theory calculations. This approach allows the reformulation of systems possessing a regular Lagrangian as Hamiltonian systems featuring a constrained phase-space dimension, characterized by a degenerate Poisson bracket. In this context, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the corresponding symplectic leaf, demonstrating that it functions as a lower-dimensional phase sub-manifold. We identify the broad conditions under which these leaves can be linear, specifically when the Lagrangian possesses significant symmetries or adopts a specific structured form. These frameworks are anticipated to hold significant utility in the construction of stable, structure-preserving algorithms. Notably, we emphasize that all described structures remain stable in field theory even in the presence of discretization errors, provided the spacetime grid remains space-like and temporal progression is sufficiently rapid, ensuring that the light cone structure is not violated by the discretization. Additionally, we investigate allometric scaling laws and their connection to the Hubble constant, providing a geometric interpretation of Hubble's law as a consequence of allometry. However, their substantial size and computational demands hinder their deployment in resource-constrained environments. Knowledge Distillation (KD) offers an effective strategy to simultaneously reduce model dimensions and enhance performance by enabling a large teacher network to train a compact student model. Yet, designing an optimal KD scheme remains challenging due to the difficulty in aligning high-dimensional outputs across different signal lengths and the lack of generalizable rules for effective distillation practices. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel and flexible distillation framework that decomposes the process into two distinct stages: signal-level and output-level distillation. By extracting complementary information from the teacher's intermediate layers and aggregating them, the proposed scheme effectively captures implicit knowledge regarding the input signal. Extensive experiments on various DCNN architectures and different length-mismatch scenarios demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves significant performance improvements. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal the critical role of each distillation component and its impact on the final results. Additionally, empirical findings indicate that the quality of distillation is influenced by the spectral characteristics of the input signal. Overall, this work provides a systematic and unified perspective on knowledge distillation and establishes a new state-of-the-art solution. It successfully accounts for the singular scaling behaviors of various thermodynamic properties near the critical temperature, adhering to the universal scaling laws established by Widom, Fisher, and Hamer. For three- and four-dimensional isotropic magnets, the analysis yields precise critical exponents and amplitude ratios. We introduce the concept of an $R$-separation for a graph $G$ based on an $R$-independent set $S$ and an $R$-independent set $T$ within the component graph of $G$ formed by removing $S$. Using this definition, we establish a four-color theorem for planar graphs. Furthermore, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for a graph to be 4-colorable. Our work generalizes and extends the findings of W.T. Gallai [1], Z.S. Song [2], W.T. Shao [3], and C.O. Christ [4].

**Definition 1.** Let $G$ be a graph and $R$ a relation on the vertex set of $G$. The component graph of $G$, denoted $\Gamma_R(G)$, is an intersection graph of the $R$-equivalence classes of $G$. If $S$ is a subset of an $R$-equivalence class, then $G - S$ refers to the component graph of $G$ after removing the $R$-equivalence class containing $S$.

**Definition 2.** An $R$-independent set $T$ in $\Gamma_R(G)$ is termed an $R$-separation of $G$ if, for every $R$-equivalence class $E$, the set $E - T$ constitutes a single $R$-equivalence class in $\Gamma_R(G) - T$.

**Theorem 1.** Let $G$ be a planar graph, $R$ a relation on $G$, $\Gamma_R(G)$ its component graph, and $T$ an $R$-separation of $G$ that is a minimal subgraph of $\Gamma_R(G)$ possessing at least three vertices. Then, there exists a planar embedding of $G$ such that the vertices of $T$ form the vertex set of a triangle in this embedding.

**Theorem 2.** Let $G$ be a planar graph, $R$ a relation on $G$, $\Gamma_R(G)$ its component graph, and $S$ an $R$-independent set in $\Gamma_R(G)$. If $S$ is a minimal graph in $\Gamma_R(G) - S$ that is an $R$-separation of $G$, then $S$ possesses at least three vertices.

However, this method relies on a specific similarity calculation that prioritizes a single dimension of ranking quality. This study introduces a novel correlation formulation where the similarity of two retrieval results is determined by the combined ranking errors they produce on a set of independent judgment queries. While these spin qubits are typically limited by low coherence due to a small gap and various charge noise sources, the development of a gate-defined ferromagnetic gate to spin-polarize the semiconductor channel introduces a new approach to achieving longer coherence times. This technique also opens avenues for a novel ferromagnet-superconductor-based topological framework. This review examines the fundamental physics of spin-coherent semimetals, reviews recent progress in spin relaxation and precession, and outlines future prospects. We demonstrate that spin coherence can be maintained in the absence of any ferromagnetic gate, and highlight that a ferromagnet-superconductor heterostructure could simultaneously exhibit the spin-momentum locking characteristic of topological insulators and the "shadow" feature specific to "proximitized" systems. Furthermore, we show that strategic placement of ferromagnetic gates allows manipulation of the "shadow" without requiring a fully ferromagnetic overlying gate. Additionally, we illustrate that spin precession can be modulated by adjusting the width of individual ferromagnetic gates, enabling a novel form of circuit-based coupling between distinct regions. Finally, we propose innovative designs to manipulate "shadow" spin textures using nonferromagnetic gates, potentially enabling new types of circuit elements essential for advanced topological quantum computation. In summary, we demonstrate that strategic use of ferromagnetic gates enables unprecedented control over spin functionalities in hybrid systems, paving the way for future research in "shadow" topological quantum computation. during labor is a standard practice for monitoring fetal well-being and detecting placenta previa and accreta. While AI is increasingly applied to automate the diagnosis of brain hemorrhages and cervical cancer, its role in evaluating pregnancy complications remains largely unexplored. This study presents a deep learning approach to automatically classify placenta previa and accreta from obstetric US videos.

**Methods:** A total of 1,080 images, gathered from eight hospitals across China, were extracted from 32 placenta previa and accreta cases and matched by a sonographer with normal pregnancies. These images were manually annotated by experienced radiologists to create a dataset of 1,080 negative (normal) and positive (abnormal) labels. We trained a two-stage model: first, a data-driven strategy to localize the region of interest (ROI) within each video using k-means clustering, and second, a ResNet-50-based classifier to distinguish between normal and abnormal placentas.

**Results:** The proposed two-stage model achieved an accuracy of 98.1%, a sensitivity of 96.3%, and a specificity of 99.9%. A five-fold cross-validation yielded an accuracy of 98.2%, a sensitivity of 95.6%, and a specificity of 99.9%. Additionally, a radiologist compared their performance (tested on 1080 cases) against our model, finding an AUC of 0.97 for the radiologist versus a 0.99 AUC for our model.

**Conclusions:** This study demonstrates that deep learning can accurately and efficiently diagnose both placenta previa and accreta. The high performance of the proposed model suggests it holds great promise for high-throughput clinical environments. Furthermore, the method's adaptability makes it suitable for diagnosing other conditions in various imaging modalities, such as obstetric and abdominal ultrasound. Finally, the method's ability to serve as a clinical support tool for healthcare workers indicates its potential to help reduce the global physician workforce shortage. **Doctor's input:** The authors have done an excellent job. statistical parametric speech synthesis. Traditional speech synthesis techniques, such as hidden Markov model-based articulatory synthesis, typically assume a Poisson distribution for phone durations. However, Poisson-based generation often results in speech that sounds overly robotic. We propose estimating speech durations according to the logistic normal distribution rather than the Poisson distribution. Although the logistic normal distribution is widely used in statistics for modeling non-negative, over-dispersed data, its application in speech synthesis has been limited. To represent this distribution, we model both the mean vector and the precision matrix of the multivariate normal distribution using Gaussian mixture models derived from speaker-dependent training data. Furthermore, we average the mean log-durations learned from male and female speakers and apply a sex-classifier to combine speech durations with acoustic features. Experimental comparisons demonstrate that our approach is more natural-sounding and significantly reduces perceived unnaturalness. These findings validate the efficacy of the logistic normal distribution in modeling multivariate speech durations with a high degree of variability. Consequently, this method holds strong potential for improving multivariate duration modeling. kidney disease (CKD) has been largely constrained by the limitations of area-wide small area studies regarding their spatial and temporal scope. This study introduces a dynamic spatially explicit model (DSEM) that incorporates spatial diffusion and temporal autocorrelation to examine CKD mortality trends. Utilizing death certificate data from the Korean National Amelioration System between 1993 and 2011, the research identifies spatial clusters exhibiting distinct temporal trends and pinpoints specific years with exceptional diffusion characteristics. Key findings include the identification of an initial CKD mortality cluster in 1993 within the central-southern Kyongsangnam-do province, followed by progressive clusters in the central Gyeongbuk and Kangwon provinces during the 2000s. This study presents a novel approach to simulate these climates by employing a new Earth System Model of Community Processes (ESMCP), termed CISM-UVic, which integrates the Community Land Model (CLM) with a simplified ocean-atmosphere box model (C2B2). The model successfully replicates ESMCP trajectories and climatic responses previously observed with coupled atmosphere-ocean general circulation models (AOGCMs). When used in coupled simulations with terrestrial carbon feedbacks, the model demonstrates a nonlinear hothouse climate response; under forced high-CO2 scenarios, the CLM 4.5 module predicts a 60% increase in global terrestrial carbon due to CO2 fertilization, while the ocean-atmosphere box model responds to both increased CO2 and higher temperatures by sequestering a net 200-300 Petagrams of Carbon (PG C). When combined, these feedbacks drive a 400–500 PG C global carbon sink, causing a transfer of carbon from the ocean to terrestrial reservoirs, which in turn lowers ocean pH and reduces the ocean's absorption capacity, thereby amplifying the hothouse climate response within the CISM-UVic framework. Under high-CO2 and warm conditions, the ESMCP structure yields a 2.5°–3.0° Celsius rise in global mean surface temperatures and lowers the global mean surface pressure by 0.3 hPa, resulting in a 1.0°–1.5° Celsius equatorial land warming relative to the coupled model's control run. Consequently, the augmented region can be substituted with a material of varying stiffness without altering the stresses within the original structure. By applying this concept, we introduce a technique to lower the effective stiffness of linear elastic structures. Specifically, we develop a method to reduce a domain's stiffness while maintaining its overall stiffness invariance. We present two novel, effect-independent variable-stiffness domains—termed "softenlets"—which are based on anisotropic and incompressible neo-Hookean models. These can be integrated into linear elastic structures to achieve significant reductions in overall stiffness while remaining blind to specific loading or boundary conditions. This study examines the influence of such factors on driving behavior by analyzing and comparing a large dataset of over 10 million events recorded from more than 5,000 fleet drivers across Europe. was developed to numerically solve autonomous dynamical systems, which serve as the basis for many applications in science and engineering. This approach relies on identifying a Koopman operator through spectral clustering on a reservoir's lifted outputs; however, the reservoir's performance is typically determined through trial and error. We demonstrate that the standard ASK technique is essentially a nearest neighbor classifier, revealing that the resolution required to accurately represent the stable manifold of the Koopman operator is driven by the need to resolve the unstable manifold of the reservoir. This insight enables the creation of an adaptive upscaling method that dynamically adjusts resolution based on the underlying manifold's properties. When applied to two model systems, this technique demonstrates that upscaling can achieve accurate low-dimensional representations of the Koopman operator without needing to know the dynamical system's specific form or parameters a priori. Additionally, we show that the method remains robust against data noise. These findings suggest that upscaling techniques are highly valuable for data-driven approaches like ASK that require high-quality, high-dimensional data. The upscaling framework is simple to implement and relies solely on estimating the Jacobian of the dynamical system at each data point, a task for which numerous efficient and robust methods already exist across various fields of science and engineering. This paves the way for upscaling techniques that can automatically determine the necessary data representation quality without requiring a priori knowledge of the system's form or parameters. Our future research will focus on generalizing these upscaling concepts to non-autonomous systems and those with unknown Koopman operators. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/jeremycaldwell/adaptive-koopman. We introduce Loyalka's method for computing pairwise distribution functions and apply it to calculate two- and three-particle distribution functions for a homogeneous, nonrelativistic Fermi gas. The resulting three-particle distribution function allows us to determine the three-body correlation sum $c_3$, an essential component of the cluster expansion for the equation of state. We also examine three-body processes within the same gas, utilizing established analytic formulas to express the relevant decay and Feshbach resonance rates as functions of the scattering length. Finally, we provide estimates for the parameter range where our findings are applicable and suggest potential extensions of our approach. Additionally, we have made available a Loyalka program designed to compute the three-body correlation sum under specific conditions. This study was conducted by a group of approximately ten physics students from the University of the Basque Country over a period of one to two months during the summer of 2019, as part of a university-wide educational initiative known as "Uni99Mezclatu," which exposes undergraduate students to emerging research topics. Our results are expected to be valuable in the emerging field of quantum simulations, which relies on controlling interactions among quantum states using highly tunable Feshbach resonances. By employing the evolution of matching coefficients and applying a large-$\alpha_s$ resummation of the logarithms generated during this process, we determine the theoretical cross-section at N$^3$LO and NNLL accuracy. Our approach begins with the leading-order hadronic cross-section, sourced from the CT18 parton distribution set. Our findings indicate that the rapidity and $x_\perp$ dependence of the evolution equations for matching coefficients is handled more comprehensively than in prior calculations. Additionally, a novel calculation of the hadronic cross-section at N$^3$LO has been performed. We observe that the resulting hadronic cross-sections align well with experimental data from the CMS and ATLAS collaborations at 13 TeV. Furthermore, the results are compared with previous calculations that included only up to NNLO corrections. Our predictions suggest that the hadronic cross-section will increase by approximately 3% relative to the NNLO result, attributed to the resummation of large logarithms associated with hadronization. The theoretical uncertainty for this calculation, assessed via the CT18 variation of alpha_s, amounts to roughly 2%. These results provide the most precise hadronic cross-section prediction to date for $t\bar{t}$ production at the LHC. The complete SCET calculation is essential for enhancing the precision of hadronized cross-section predictions in proton-proton collisions at the LHC. This work advances the understanding of resummation effects in hadronization and offers a robust theoretical foundation for the interpretation of future top-quark data. The code and data necessary to reproduce our calculations are available for download. This marks the most precise SCET calculation yet for the hadronic cross-section in $t\bar{t}$ production at the LHC. The code and data to reproduce our calculations are provided for access. However, simply measuring mobility is insufficient; understanding its nature, patterns, and characteristics is equally important for gaining a deeper insight into urban economies. This study examines the nature of mobility within a city using data from 13.5 million users of 10.7 million rides. We introduce a set of metrics to characterize mobility, including its size, scaling, heterogeneity, temporal attributes, and spatio-temporal distributions. Our findings reveal that daily mobility volume is inherently scale-free, meaning it lacks a characteristic size. Additionally, we observe that size bias tends to mask the true scaling behavior of real-world systems. Consequently, we propose an unbiased scaling index to accurately describe size-independent mobility characteristics. Ultimately, this research offers fundamental insights into mobility that can facilitate more accurate and effective prediction and management of urban economies. By understanding daily mobility nature, we aim to enhance urban services and foster economic development. Furthermore, this work addresses a fundamental question in urban economics: what drives daily mobility sizes? Understanding this can lead to improved management of daily mobility, ultimately benefiting essential services and the broader urban economy. Finally, we demonstrate that the daily mobility size follows a power-law distribution across various cities and time periods. This distribution indicates that differentiating between small and large mobility events is arbitrary, as no distinct event size exists. Consequently, we argue that understanding and characterizing daily mobility nature is fundamental to accurately forecasting and managing daily mobility patterns. Additionally, we provide a theoretical explanation for this scale-free behavior, deriving it from the Poisson process. Through this framework, we establish that the mobility cascade is a fundamental characteristic of daily mobility. Ultimately, this research provides a foundation for accurately predicting future mobility sizes. Moreover, we show that the bias index for characterizing daily mobility nature remains consistent across different cities and time periods, indicating that daily mobility nature is relatively stable and stable over time. Consequently, these results can be effectively utilized to forecast future mobility sizes. Finally, we validate the universality of these results across diverse cities and time periods, confirming the consistency of these findings in various contexts. In conclusion, by understanding the daily mobility size through this lens, we can significantly improve prediction and management of urban mobility services and contribute to fostering the development of urban economies. This study examines topological planar vortex arrays featuring chiral dislocations as a specific instance of chiral geometry. We demonstrate that the platelet number uniquely defines these vortex arrays. Arrays classified as number-platelet-chiral (NPC) exhibit topological chirality, whereas array-platelet-chiral (APC) arrays display parity-breaking geometrical chirality. Both VC and APC arrays possess a complete set of topological invariants that fully capture their topological properties. This behavior has been observed in both humans and animals, yet its persistence is often attributed simply to the difficulty of overcoming it. We propose an alternative explanation: an ecological rationality argument suggesting that probability-matching may be optimal for a distinct class of learners when the environment changes over time. Specifically, the challenge involves receiving $n$ binary vectors of dimension $d$, followed by queries for pairs of vectors within a distance of $r=\lfloor\epsilon d\rfloor$, returning them with a probability of at least $1-c$. We introduce a new encoding technique for binary vectors and develop a randomized algorithm to address this problem. Our results demonstrate that for any constant $\epsilon > 0$ and $d\gg n$, an algorithm exists with query time of $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2} d^{2/3} n^{1/3})$ and an approximation factor $c$ approaching zero as $\epsilon$ decreases. This represents a substantial improvement over previous methods, which lacked dependence on $n$ but required $\epsilon$ to be near zero. Additionally, we present an algorithm with query time of $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon d^{2/3} n^{1/3})$ where $c$ remains a constant. These performance metrics mark significant progress toward the first all-pairs $O(d)$ encoding. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound proving that no randomized algorithm can achieve query times better than $\widetilde{\Omega}(\epsilon d/n)$. Finally, we compare our findings with the fastest deterministic algorithms. By adapting Borwein's encoding for symmetric difference detection, we propose an alternative randomized approach with query time of $\widetilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2} d \sqrt{n})$ where $c$ approaches zero as $\epsilon$ approaches zero. This improvement demonstrates that randomization offers an asymptotic advantage over deterministic algorithms. To our knowledge, this work presents the first substantial advancement in near neighbor algorithms since Indyk's breakthrough. It advances the understanding of the first $L_2$ embedding and offers new insights into Borwein's encoding. Our findings also contribute to understanding the power of randomization in this context. Results from both models are compared against each other and against those of two fully separated plates. This work introduces a unified framework that integrates machine learning with traditional modeling techniques to construct data-based predictive models for dynamical systems. The approach begins by decomposing the system dynamics into two components: (1) a machine learning component that captures dynamics within a finite, bounded input domain, and (2 a "correction term" that accounts for discrepancies arising from machine learning approximation errors and dynamics outside the bounded domain. The correction term is derived from training data using an inverse problem formulation. The resulting model comprises two parts: the output from the machine learning model and the solution to the inverse problem. This combination yields a data-driven model blending the interpretability of traditional modeling approaches with the flexibility and accuracy of machine learning. The method is demonstrated by developing predictive models for various dynamical systems, including Lorenz attractors, the van der Pol oscillator, and a supersonic axial-flow compressor, which also highlights the model's applicability in predicting complex phenomena like thermoacoustic instabilities. The resulting models enhance understanding of system dynamics, improve prediction accuracy, and serve as inputs for optimization and control strategies. This study examines PBHs within the framework of non-minimally derivative couplings (NMDC), a mechanism involving derivatives of the scalar field kinetic term. Under this paradigm, evaporation via Hawking radiation causes their mass to diminish over time, necessitating initial masses in the critical range. The investigation focuses on three subtypes of NMDC couplings. Results indicate that only the second subtype allows PBHs with initial masses of $10^{15}$ g to survive to the present day, whereas the third subtype predicts evaporation rates exceeding those of the second. Furthermore, assuming complete dark matter composition of these PBHs, their existence imposes a constraint on the inflationary potential's NMDC coefficient, indicating it must be significantly smaller than unity. Additionally, this requirement suggests that any observable primordial black clouds would be extremely faint. Finally, the impact of these NMDC couplings on the formation of supermassive black holes is also explored. Ultimately, the conclusion is that the cosmological scenario involving PBHs as dark matter is best described by the second NMDC subtype, which can also address the $U(1)_{em}$ hierarchy problem. $\odot$ 2021. the equation of state, phase behavior, and transport properties of a simple polymer melt containing a planar interface with a gas phase. These systems represent the deposed state of a polymer melt, serving as fundamental models for understanding the drying process and the resulting evaporated surfaces. To simulate the evaporated surface, we maintained a constant vapor pressure while gradually lowering the temperature. The resulting nonequilibrium surfaces matched those obtained from equilibrium simulations at identical interface conditions. We then performed off-equilibrium diffusion measurements, calculating the diffusion coefficient as the ratio of the mean square displacement to time. This yielded two distinct diffusion coefficients: a bulk value near the interface and a value within the surface layer itself. By comparing these results with those from the equilibrium Einstein relation, we demonstrated that the nonequilibrium findings accurately reflect the effects of drying on polymer surfaces. Finally, we utilized the findings from this study, alongside molecular dynamics simulations of a polystyrene melt, to propose a revised expression for the square of the correlation length. This new expression incorporates a single material-dependent fitting parameter and offers improved agreement with existing experimental and simulation data. Furthermore, we found that the exponent $\xi_{\perp}$ in the scaling law for the out-of-plane correlation length, $\xi_{\perp}\sim\left|\ T-T_c\right|^{-\xi_{\perp}}$, is approximately 1.15, aligning with previous literature. We also determined the exponent for the order parameter amplitude $M_{\perp}$ and provided data for the exponent $\xi_{\parallel}$ related to the parallel correlation length $\xi_{\parallel}\sim\left| T-T_c\right|^{-\xi_{\parallel}}$. Additionally, the critical temperature $T_c$ and the amplitude of the order parameter $M_M$ were derived, enabling the construction of a phase diagram for the polymer melt vapor-liquid interface. This study represents the first to simultaneously examine the scaling of both the parallel and out-of-plane correlation lengths in a polymer melt interface. Due to the accessible and adjustable nature of these systems, the methodology can be readily extended to other polymers and their blends. Such an extension would facilitate the creation of detailed phase diagrams for a wide range of polymers, including those with drying applications. These diagrams are essential for the rational design of materials with optimized evaporated surfaces. In conclusion, the proposed study serves as a practical guide for applying molecular simulations to examine the out-of-equilibrium dynamics of polymer melts and their resulting evaporated surfaces. Transformer models frequently depend on inductive biases to perform specific tasks. This paper introduces a methodology for explicitly identifying such biases, termed Bias Fingerprints. This framework not only reveals particular traits of pre-trained transformers, such as their preference for shorter input sequences, but also suggests practical applications, including optimizing hyperparameters to minimize data requirements. Furthermore, we explore how to incorporate certain biases, like factuality and consistency, to enhance real-world utility. We introduce a method for automatically generating explanations for pre-trained language models by utilizing in-context learning within a second language model. This approach eliminates the need for a separate explanatory model's parameters, streamlining the explanation generation process. By employing this framework, we offer two key recommendations for future research: ensuring diversity in intervention points and providing in-distribution examples during self-explanation generation. This framework also facilitates the investigation of other desirable qualities in explainable models. Consequently, we highlight the importance of ensuring reasoning capabilities in explainable models and offer advice on enhancing them. Our results demonstrate that pre-trained explainable models can achieve competitive performance on various reasoning benchmarks. This paper investigates the implications of such high-mass particles, specifically focusing their impact through quantum corrections to the beta function of a coupled field. These quantum corrections can substantially alter inflationary predictions, even when the number of such high-mass particles is relatively small. We demonstrate that a single particle species can significantly modify predictions from various features, thereby influencing model building. Consequently, a careful analysis of the influence exerted by heavy particles on inflationary predictions is essential. Furthermore, we present a technique for incorporating the effects of heavy particles and apply it to scenarios involving features and to the radiative correction-based generation of features. We illustrate that quantum corrections from heavy particles can markedly improve the amplitude of feature-induced fluctuations. As a demonstration, we examine the minimal alignment model and demonstrate that the predicted tensor mode amplitude can be greatly enhanced by the quantum effects of heavy particles. This finding offers a viable strategy for resolving tension between inflationary predictions and Planck observations regarding the tensor mode amplitude. Constructing such a scenario with heavy particles and presenting detailed predictions will be the focus of a subsequent paper. Additionally, we demonstrate that quantum corrections from heavy particles can substantially increase the duration of pre-inflationary oscillations of the inflaton field, which is relevant for cyclic inflation models. Finally, we discuss that heavy particles can significantly affect the post-inflationary universe, potentially influencing the nucleosynthesis era. In summary, the contributions of heavy particles to inflational landscapes are substantial and must be incorporated into both model construction and the comparison of theoretical predictions with observational data. Given that the radiative correction method represents a promising approach for feature model building, a comprehensive discussion of the effects of heavy particles will be presented in a future paper.

Yet, creating meaningful visual explanations for deep learning techniques remains difficult because of the domain's inherent complexity and swift pace of innovation. Consequently, we seek visual methods that can adapt to evolving machine learning paradigms. While saliency maps have traditionally been employed to reveal how inputs influence outputs, we argue that the diverse strategies used to generate these maps hinder the creation of versatile explanations. Our findings indicate that latent space parameterization offers a novel perspective for interpreting visual tasks, particularly in complex scenarios like image synthesis and variational autoencoders, where even the most elementary concepts remain elusive. Furthermore, visualizing the latent action space of an autoencoder and examining it via clustering distances helps (1) understand how the model constructs simple structures like shapes and textures in generated images and (2) investigate the impact of minor variations in adversarial examples on adversarial robustness. Ultimately, our results highlight the potential of latent space visualization for interpreting visual tasks while exposing critical blind spots within the images produced by generative models. This study examines the cuprate system as a highly correlated electron-phonon model, specifically analyzing the effects of phonons that are Raman-active across all Bragg peaks, with the aim of achieving an Mott insulating transition. We specifically investigate whether the transverse mode $B_{1g}$ provides a viable mechanism for high-temperature superconductivity by employing a microscopically self-consistent technique to solve the model near the Mott transition. Our findings demonstrate that the $B_{1g}$ mode successfully explains key experimental phenomena, including low-energy spectral weight, the cuprate phase diagram, the joint density of states, the anomalous resistivity observed in optimally doped samples, and the characteristic dome shape of superconducting $T_c$ in cuprates. By comparing multiple theoretical techniques, we offer insights into the computational methods and numerical approaches used in electron-phonon simulations. Ultimately, we conclude that transverse $B_{1g}$ phonons can serve as a plausible mechanism for high-temperature superconductivity near the Mott transition. These results also imply that electron-phonon coupling must be treated non-perturbatively and suggest that superconductivity in cuprates exhibits a strong energy dependence at low temperatures. Additionally, we provide evidence supporting a metallic state at zero phonon coupling. To our knowledge, this represents the first self-consistent many-body electron-phonon simulation demonstrating that the $B_{1g}$ phonon mode can explain high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates. We contend that our findings warrant further experimental validation. Given that similar mechanisms may apply to other high-$T_c$ superconductors, our results warrant broader investigation. Finally, the methodologies presented here can be extended to explain high-temperature superconductivity in other materials, such as $\text{MgB}_2$, Fe-based superconductors, and $\text{CaC}_6$. In conclusion, our theoretical analysis indicates that transverse $B_{1g}$ phonons can explain high-temperature superconductivity near the Mott transition in cuprates. Both materials demonstrate robust room-temperature chiral magnetic ordering, with CMW exhibiting one of the highest transition temperatures ($T_c$) among oxide magnets. Neutron diffraction and bulk measurements show that CMW maintains a $T_c$ of approximately 600 K and a saturation moment of 0.5 $\mu_B$/f.u. Notably, CMW and BBW display distinct temperature dependencies in the magnitude of their chiral order parameter, which peaks near 300 K for CMW and 100 K for BBW. To explain these variations, we propose that a competition between a spin-screw order along the $c$ axis and a spin-ring order within the $ab$ plane governs the spin structure in these materials.

This study examines the validity of such turbulence through numerical simulations of dynamos within identical convective shells, comparing the impacts of buoyancy-driven turbulence versus shear-driven turbulence. Both turbulence types were generated by imposing a stochastic source term on velocity within numerically indistinguishable setups. The investigation reveals that the efficacy of the classical tachocline dynamo is unaffected by the source of turbulence, thereby contradicting the hypothesis that turbulent transport necessarily suppresses dynamo activity. Furthermore, we investigated dynamos relying on Omega-effect twist and the Omega-effect dynamo, confirming that the tachocle dynamon mechanism operates in both scenarios and remains unchanged by the presence of either turbulence type. Our findings indicate that the specific origin of the turbulence is a critical factor, yet the resulting mean magnetic field structures are remarkably similar regardless of whether the turbulence arises from buoyancy or the tachocla itself. These results stem from high-resolution (O(NI06)) simulations of a dynamical dynamo model based on mean-field magnetohydrodynamics, encompassing 24 distinct runs, where NI06 denotes the grid size of the tachocle region. The optimal magnetic field configurations emerge when the dynamo is driven by both tachocla shear and bulk turbulence, resulting in saturated states characterized by weak, disordered magnetic fields. These outcomes are interpreted as a consequence of the dynamical interaction between magnetic helicity and angular momentum flux, alongside the suppression of mean fields by small-scale, coherent flows. The most promising configurations arise when the tachocla shear exceeds the level of bulk turbulence, as the tachocla dynamo mechanism suppresses the mean magnetic field in this regime. These findings align with observed sunspot data, which indicate that the tachocla shear is stronger than the turbulence in the convection zone, thereby suppressing convection from penetrating into the tachocla. Results indicate that the proposed method outperforms the well-established Newton-Ginzburg-Landau nonlinear Schrödinger equation (GNLSTE) in handling wideband scenarios. This approach offers superior accuracy compared to the GNLSTE for wideband cases, effectively solving challenges typically associated with closed-form analytical methods like Laguerre polynomials. Finally, the algorithm is extended to model the nonlinear wave equation for electron plasma waves by incorporating an envelope transformation and applying superposition operators to finite-dimensional vector-structured matrices, achieving remarkable performance in this extended application as well. Overall, the nonlinear algorithm achieves significantly lower numerical dispersion and absorption than the GNLSTE, exhibiting excellent capabilities for very wideband cases. These solution-aided modeling techniques offer substantial potential for enhancing the accuracy of electromagnetic system simulations. Future research will focus on improving solution accuracy for wide-open boundary conditions in solution-domain based-electromagnetic system modeling. Additionally, the authors intend to extend solution-dominant algorithms to accelerate the solution of the averaged Vlasov-Maxwell equations, thereby significantly reducing the computational cost of solution-domain based-electromagnetic system modeling. However, critics often argue that outperforming such a broad benchmark is relatively simple because the benchmark's breadth causes excessive dispersion, allowing active managers to easily find superior assets. This paper introduces and examines the MSCI Euronext, a narrower, more concentrated alternative to the standard index. Our findings indicate that when the benchmark is the more concentrated MSCI Euronext, the validity of the traditional active management arguments—specifically that a "smart" manager can outperform a concentrated but "dumb" portfolio—weakens. Consequently, we advocate for a more rigorous, albeit challenging, benchmark in which genuine claims of outperformance can be credibly asserted. Furthermore, we conclude by analyzing the implications for accurately measuring true skill. Specifically, we show that if the true skill portfolio (the true Markowitz portfolio) allocates negative weights to certain assets, then the standard manager is likely to be overworked, leading to a high probability of underperformance. In contrast, the more concentrated "dumb" portfolio is likely to be overworked in a different context, which helps explain why the number of underperformers is not significantly higher than the number of outperformers. Ultimately, the more concentrated benchmark and the resulting lower weight dispersion make it harder to find assets that clearly outperform the "dumb" portfolio. Furthermore, the number of "smart" managers who can outperform a less challenging benchmark is likely to be smaller than previously thought. We also show how the MSCI Euronext can serve as a starting point for constructing even more concentrated and "dumb" portfolios, such as the MSCI Euronext 50. Finally, we demonstrate how the smart/"dumb" spread can be calculated for various markets, revealing that the issue is particularly severe in smaller markets like Israel and South Korea. Finally, we show how the size of the market and its associated risks are strongly correlated with the smart/"dumb" spread. We conclude by arguing that this correlation supports the use of a "smart/dumb" metric as a proxy for measuring the true size and risk of a market. Finally, we show how the size and risk of a market can help explain why more managers outperform in larger and riskier markets than in smaller and safer ones. Furthermore, we argue that because larger and riskier markets are harder to outperform, less money should be managed in their names. Conversely, since smaller and safer markets are easier to outperform, more money should be managed in their names. We

The Landau-Zener transition probability governing the creation of quasiparticles decays exponentially as bond disorder increases, yet it remains robust against disorder affecting the fermionic site potential, and follows a power-law dependence on boson disorder. By employing a coarse-grained density functional theory, the authors analyze the density profile of a non-interacting bosonic chain in the deep localization regime; this profile is entirely determined by the initial wavefunction and the time-averaged on-site energy. The study's results are supported by numerical simulations. Furthermore, the authors examine a theoretical issue concerning the interpretation of the density profile as an effective potential and explore the problem of calculating the density profile's wavefunction in the event of a node. To address these issues, the coarsening process is reinterpreted as a time-dependent nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring a time-varying chemical constant, which is solved numerically. Additionally, the node problem is resolved by applying a node removal procedure to the continuous wavefunction during the coarsening process. Finally, the authors calculate the participation ratio of the wavefunction resulting from node removal and compare it with other methods, such as the continued fraction expansion. This methodology is also applied to the study of a disordered boson model involving dimerization and a potential difference between even and odd sites. The continuation of this study will explore a model featuring an emergent symmetry-breaking mechanism in the disordered phase. Specifically, at strong disorder and low temperatures, a dimerization pattern emerges, resulting in an effective Hamiltonian with a smaller unitary cell and a participation ratio that differs from the deep localization limit. This work will provide insight into the nature of the many-body localized phase and its relationship to the Landau-Zener diagram. The anticipated continuation is scheduled for the near future. By imposing the asymptotic alignment limit on couplings between the leptophilic scalar and top quarks, we achieve top-quark production at the LHC that is nearly independent of the leptophilic scalar. This independence allows top-quark observables, such as the cross-section, to remain unperturbed by leptonic effects, thereby enabling precise top-quark measurements even in the presence of leptophilic scalars. Furthermore, we derive a lower bound on the leptophilic scalar mass, determined by the running of the flavour-diagonal Yukawa couplings of charged leptons. Finally, we examine the potential for asymptotic alignment in the up sector at infinite energy and conclude that it cannot be realized. Consequently, we suggest a similar bound on the leptophilic scalar mass if up-type flavour-changing neutral currents are present in the UV sector. This suggests an optimal strategy for new physics searches at the high-energy LHC: although top-quark production remains hard processes, its precision can be ensured through the relatively simple flavour structure inherent in the SM. In this context, the new physics sector functions as a "theoretical laboratory," where rigorous theoretical constraints significantly simplify experimental searches. This represents a novel perspective on LHC searches that complements the traditional focus solely on the quantity of top-quark data. Our findings also have practical implications for LHCb and other experimental searches. Extending this logic, we note that the unification of asymptotic charged lepton mass ratios is also possible in the down sector, thereby constraining flavour-violating interactions mediated by leptophilic scalars at the energy scales of that sector. In this specific case, the new physics sector acts as a "theoretical telescope," allowing us to observe beyond the LHC's energy limits. These results may inspire new theoretical and experimental proposals tailored for upcoming experimental facilities. In this regard, we observe that our work opens a pathway for precise measurements of the Higgs boson mass using top-quark data, despite the complicated flavour structure present at the electroweak scale. We emphasize that this represents a new approach to searching for new physics using the top quark. Additionally, we suggest an alternative method to directly measure the Higgs boson mass without any theoretical uncertainties, utilizing the same logic applied here. Our findings may also guide a new search for the dark matter particle at direct detection experiments, leveraging the flavour structure of the leptophilic scalar model. We

This paper presents a distributed interference alignment algorithm designed for a two-cell cognitive radio network. In this setup, each cell contains multiple unlicensed users sharing a frequency band with cells of cognitive users, while each cognitive radio cell is equipped with a small number of aligned precoders. Specifically, we derive a distributed precoder design based on the ADMM framework. Unlike prior work, this approach eliminates the need for exact knowledge of local channel matrices and avoids the high complexity of a centralized matrix inversion ADMM procedure. Instead, it leverages the distributability of ADMM to generate a decentralized algorithm with reduced complexity. We demonstrate that this method converges to a stationary point of the global interference alignment ADMM problem. Numerical results indicate that this precoder design outperforms existing schemes in both distributed interference alignment success rates and ADMM complexity. Crucially, it utilizes only a minimal number of cognitive radio users per cell, thereby maximizing spectral efficiency. Furthermore, we prove that the proposed algorithm ensures no illegal user is blocked from the network, and all legitimate users achieve their target rates. Simulations confirm that the proposed precoder design effectively guarantees fair spectrum access for all illegal users. Our findings reveal that the proposed design achieves an average increased success rate for illegal users by approximately 10% to 100% compared to existing methods. Consequently, this precoder design offers a promising and practical solution for future wireless networks to enhance spectral efficiency. In summary, the proposed design enables fair spectrum access and improves overall spectral efficiency within a multi-cell cognitive radio environment. The paper begins by introducing the two-cell cognitive radio network and then proceeds to derive the distributed precoder design. Finally, it demonstrates the numerical performance of the proposed method and compares it against existing approaches. Furthermore, the results show that the proposed precoder design enhances the overall spectral efficiency of the cognitive radio network by utilizing a small number of cognitive radio users per cell. Additionally, the proposed design guarantees fair spectrum access, and simulations confirm that it increases the success rate of illegal users by 10% to 100% relative to existing schemes. Therefore, the proposed precoder design effectively ensures fair spectrum access within a two-cell cognitive radio network. Finally, the proposed cognitive radio precoder design utilizes a small number of cognitive radio users per cell, thereby enhancing the overall spectral efficiency of the network. In summary, the proposed precoder design ensures fair spectrum access and increases the overall spectral efficiency

By integrating GPDs with parton helicity distributions and spin-dependent deep inelastic scattering (SDIS) observables within a unified GPD framework, a partial deconstruction of the nucleon's spin and impact on flavor separation has been achieved. Leveraging the constrained GPD sets derived from next-to-leading-order QCD fits to existing data, this study calculates predictions for spin-dependent deep inelastic scattering at a future electron-ion collider. The results indicate that GPD analysis can be advanced using relatively modest experimental datasets from the proposed EIC. Furthermore, this emerging information will enhance global QCD analyses of nucleon spin, eventually enabling a complete flavor and spatial decomposition of the nucleon's spin. Finally, we explore the connections between these GPDs and other nucleon properties probed at the EIC, including transverse spatial charge distributions, generalized form factors, and twist-3 twistering. Through this comprehensive GPD analysis of the nucleon, we reveal that the quark contribution to the nucleon spin is more distributed than previously thought. Prior to our work, neither the probabilistic nor the asymptotic characteristics of optima derived from well-behaved kernels had been thoroughly examined. This study investigates the probabilistic behavior of optima associated with "poorly-behaved" kernels—those that are positively defined but not positive definite. We demonstrate that even with these suboptimal kernels, out-of-sample performance can remain excellent, contingent on the test data distribution. By employing both the explicit "cusp" loss landscape and "neural tangent" kernel construction, we reveal that optima exist in low-loss regions that are both globally stable and dynamically robust, exhibiting stability that exceeds what the loss landscape alone suggests. Furthermore, we show that these low-loss regions can be predicted a priori based on the kernel, the training data and labels, and distinct predictions regarding test data. The dynamics governing the evolution of these regions also exhibit greater stability than anticipated from the kernels' positive-definiteness. These findings offer critical insights into the artificial intelligence of machines utilizing kernels that are technically flawed from both theoretical and practical perspectives. Ultimately, this research underscores that achieving optimal artificial intelligence does not necessitate possessing optimal artificial intelligence.

This study examines a two-dimensional Fermi gas subjected to ultralow-energy interactions driven by spin-orbit coupling (SOC). We demonstrate that incorporating even weak momentum-dependent momentum and momentum-momentum interactions can significantly suppress the system's effective dimensionality. We introduce a field-theoretic framework based on the one-loop self-energy correction to the propagator within the EFT300 regulator scheme of EFT+ to analyze these higher-order SOC effects. Additionally, we identify a stabilizing renormalization group (RG) flow for EFT300 that enables the systematic exploration of systems approaching zero dimensionality. Numerical one-particle density of states calculations reveal that EFT300 systems exhibit infrared divergences characteristic of one-dimensional systems at flows reaching RG scales as low as $\Lambda_{\text{max}}/10$. Furthermore, we find that EFT300 systems display Luttinger liquid behavior, which we associate with the emergence of emergent Majorana fermions. Our study confirms that EFT+ at the EFT300 EFT+ order can effectively capture the physics of systems with extremely low dimensionality. This finding suggests that EFT+ is suitable for describing novel quantum phases induced by unusual momentum-dependent interactions, such as quantum spin liquids and quantum phase slips, without needing to explicitly construct emergent degrees of freedom. The EFT300 we develop may offer a pathway to experimentally observe quantum systems with zero dimensionality. We also outline the theoretical implications for many-body systems with highly momentum-dependent interactions. The EFT300 LLL order could serve as a useful theoretical tool for understanding momentum-dependent interactions and exploring the physics of quasi-one-dimensional quantum systems. Consequently, the conventional t-statistic becomes sensitive to estimation errors in these few components and fails the Hannan-Rissanen condition, leading to the inflation of actual type-I error rates beyond nominal levels. Specifically, the first stage generates two sets of test statistics incorporating distinct types of robustness to first-order correlation; the second stage evaluates significance using a novel wild cluster bootstrap method that further relaxes assumptions regarding weak dependence and spatial heterogeneity to ensure accurate inference. Simulation studies demonstrate significant type-I error rate distortions in standard procedures, which our proposed method effectively corrects. Furthermore, the method performs well in comparative finite sample experiments when tested against alternative recent techniques. We also apply this approach to assess district-level interventions across two different time periods. A key contribution of this paper is the development of valid statistical inference capable of handling first-order correlation structures found in standard difference-in-differences estimators, even under complex and highly non-standard correlation and heterogeneity conditions. Additionally, this method performs effectively even when type-I error distortions are absent in certain specific scenarios. All supporting code is available on GitHub. [ArXiv:2103.01514]

for numerous astrophysical topics, including stellar population synthesis, the chemical enrichment of galaxies, and the formation theories of clusters and galaxies. However, cluster parameters are often difficult to determine accurately, particularly in large and extended clusters where the distinction between members and foreground/background stars is unclear. While the most robust parameter estimation relies on dynamical data, such data are scarce for the majority of clusters. Consequently, photometry serves as the most common method for estimating these parameters. This study employs machine learning algorithms to identify the precise radial velocity cutoff that separates cluster members from non-members within the Coma Berenices cluster. By utilizing Gaia photometric data, we train a Support Vector Machine (SVM) to find this cutoff threshold, thereby facilitating the estimation of various physical parameters for the cluster. Additionally, we present the results of applying our method to four other star clusters. Finally, we discuss utilizing this approach to constrain the age of the Milky Way galaxy. This research represents a preliminary effort to develop a novel technique for estimating cluster parameters using photometry alone, potentially opening a new avenue for future studies.
