While a comprehensive analytical approach to subjectivity measures for binary images (representing Markov random field excursions) was absent until recently, the novel method proposed by P. Forger and E. Zaidenfield offers a solution, yielding formulas for entropy and subjectivity. However, calculating these values directly via the method's original way is computationally expensive in practice. We reframe the process of determining subjectivity by transforming it into a problem of maximizing entropy under specific constraints, thereby enabling the development of efficient algorithms to generate and analyze grayscale images representing binary patterns. This study derives the first-order and second-order constraints and their higher-order extensions from the definition of subjectivity and entropy for P. Forger and E. Zaidenfield's model. Finally, we present numerical examples comparing standard methods with the constrained entropy maximization (CEM) method, demonstrating that CEM more effectively preserves key characteristics and significantly reduces complexity. Additionally, we apply this technique to generate canonical images of specific binary patterns using Monte Carlo simulations with CEM. The findings indicate that Monte Carlo simulations based on this approach successfully produce grayscale images highly characteristic of the original binary images, even after substantial smoothing. We also provide specific parameters and the number of Monte Carlo steps recommended for practical implementation. Numerical results show that, depending on the binary image's structure, convergence to the true solution of the Monte Carlo simulation can be achieved with as few as 10 to 200 iterations. Finally, we demonstrate that Monte Carlo simulations solve the CEM problem exactly using the Hit-and-Run algorithm, which is equivalent to performing a single iteration of the algorithm on the original problem space without smoothing. Furthermore, we show that this approach can be extended to scenarios where the prior probability distribution of patterns is not uniform. etric Interferometer for Astrophysics) is an ESA mission designed to create the most extensive and accurate three-dimensional map of the Galaxy, offering over one billion high-precision astrometric and photometric observations of nearly all bright stars within 15 kiloparsecs. This article provides a comprehensive overview of Gaia's scientific mission and presents the initial findings from its first data release. By combining astrometry, photometry, and spectroscopy, Gaia enables an extensive array of Galactic astrophysics investigations. Among these, one specific method involves utilizing the rotation curve of the thin disc to measure the disc's gravitational potential, thereby deriving the superimposed dark matter density. The proposed method relies on analyzing the proper motions of stars to determine the disc's gravitational potential and, subsequently, the dark matter density; this approach utilizes the observed proper motions of main-sequence stars to infer the disc's gravitational potential and calculate the dark matter density. The study determines the dark matter density to be $0.56 \pm 0.10 \; M_{\odot} \; \text{pc}^{-3}$ at a distance of 8.2 kpc from the Galactic centre. Additionally, the paper addresses challenges in interpreting the rotation curve of the thin disc and suggests methodologies for overcoming these obstacles. Limitations of the current study are highlighted, and future research directions are proposed. While the proposed method serves as a significant contribution to the field, it is noted that the sensitivity of the method can be further enhanced by incorporating more precise and numerous observations provided by the Gaia mission. This suggests that more accurate results can be achieved in forthcoming investigations that utilize Gaia's data. To conclude, I aim to express my gratitude for the opportunity to contribute to this remarkable mission. Specifically, to accurately measure the disc's rotation curve using Gaia's proper motion data, it is essential to account for the Sun's motion relative to the Galactic centre, the disc's rotation curve, and the influence of the Galactic disc's spiral arms on star trajectories. Additionally, the distribution of stars along the line of sight should be considered to achieve more accurate results. Finally, the sensitivity of the proposed method is expected to improve significantly with a larger volume of observations from the second and third data releases of the Gaia mission. Leveraging Gaia's observations will facilitate more precise determination of the dark matter density within the Galactic thin disc. Our approach achieves $O(n+\alpha\log\alpha)$ time, where $n$ denotes the size of the lists and $\alpha$ represents the number of inversions within a specific block of the list. The algorithm's runtime can be further optimized to $O(n + \text{inv}(L_1) + \text{inv}(L_2))$, where $\text{inv}(L_i)$ corresponds to the total number of inversions in list $L_i$. We provide a proof for this claim and present the necessary word-RAM techniques, which may have broader applications. Additionally, we demonstrate how to calculate the mean rank correlation, a variant of the standard measure, within the same asymptotic time complexity. Our implementation surpasses the performance of the implementation provided by Sagemath's Combinatorics package, the primary open-source alternative. A comprehensive experimental evaluation not only confirms the theoretical results but also compares the algorithm against other state-of-the-art implementations, accounting for the overheads inherent in high-level languages. The code is accessible via Sagemath, and we include a detailed discussion of the algorithms used in those open-source packages. The accompanying video demonstrates a rigorous experimental comparison, including worst-case scenarios, between our implementation and those found in existing open-source libraries. Our finding demonstrates that the $k$-th eigenvalue scales proportionally to $\max\{k, n/p\}$, where $k$ denotes the index of the eigenvalue (assumed $k < n/p \ll 1$), $n$ represents the sample size, and $p$ the dimensionality. Compared to prior results derived from matrix concentration inequalities, our approach leverages a more refined analysis of the spectral norm of random random design design matrices, yielding a significantly tighter bound in scenarios where $k$ scales logarithmically with $n/p$ (i.e., $k < C\log(n/p)$ for some constant $C$). Simulations using the identity covariance matrix and various popular covariance structures, where $p$ is large and $n/p$ is moderate, indicate that our lower bound is nearly tight. Furthermore, we extend these results to settings with non-isotropic covariance. While existing literature primarily addresses asymptotic regimes with fixed noise variance, our analysis introduces novel techniques applicable to varying covariance structures and design types. Additionally, the methodology can be adapted using an alternative approach to derive analogous lower bounds even when $n/p$ does not constitute a moderate quantity. Simulation studies support the finding that our bounds are tight across a broad spectrum of hyperparameters. The associated $\mathbb{R}$ code, titled \emph{\textcolor{blue}{\url{https://github.com/zhengyelee/LevLowerBound}}}, is publicly available. Finally, we also examine a complementary problem, formulating a non-asymptotic upper bound on the estimation error using the least squares estimator. Simulations reveal that this upper bound is tight for specific hyperparameters. The code used to generate these results is included in the repository. To the best of our knowledge, this work presents the first non-asymptotic bounds on the spectral distribution of random design design matrices. The primary contributions are (i) the derivation of these bounds and (ii) the extension to non-isotropic covariance structures. In this context, an adversarial example is a naturally classified input that has been subtly altered to cause a classifier to produce a different classification than intended. Driven by the desire to enhance the robustness of classification models, numerous attacks and defenses have been developed in recent years. Within the domain of Natural Language Processing (NLP), researchers have long sought to build robust systems, with recent efforts specifically targeting NPW vulnerabilities. agents perceive and interact with their environment. Central to this process is the brain's hypothesis-testing mechanism, which utilizes an internal model to guide behavior. Recent mathematical formulations of active inference have highlighted the importance of free energy minimization, specifically targeting both perception and action. Although the integration of belief updating with active inference is well-established in existing literature, this work presents a comprehensive derivation of a dynamic active inference model to facilitate in-depth analysis. We conduct a thorough exploration of the mathematical underpinnings of this framework to support robust theoretical investigation. Additionally, we derive the continuous-time equivalent of the model to enable robust analysis based on the specific characteristics of neural dynamics. Our primary contribution lies in providing a unified view of the field by consolidating various formulations into a single, rigorous framework. This approach not only aids in elucidating the mathematical structure of active inference but also establishes a basis for future research to expand the theory and refine its applications. Furthermore, we demonstrate how active inference can be interpreted through Bayesian learning, a perspective that will be utilized to conduct extensive theoretical analysis. Leveraging these theorems, we perform detailed investigations into the behavior of active inference, employing tools such as dynamical systems theory and algebraic geometry. These analytical methods yield insights into system equilibria and the stability of such states within the context of active inference. Finally, we apply these findings to investigate how the characteristics of the environment and the agent's neural dynamics influence equilibrium behavior. This analysis reveals the conditions necessary for an agent to adaptively modify its behavior in response to environmental challenges. Additionally, we examine the impact of various functional forms of the Q-function on equilibrium behavior, offering insights into agent adaptability and learning within this theoretical framework. Through this comprehensive investigation, we aim to provide a detailed understanding of dynamic active inference, a resource that will support future learning and extension of the theory. We anticipate that this research will assist in advancing the understanding of dynamic active inference and encourage further developments within this exciting and emerging field. This paper serves as the authors' doctoral dissertation, submitted to the University of Tokyo in 2022. The research was initially published as two back-to-back articles in IEEE Transactions on Cognitive and Developmental Systems (2022) and subsequently expanded into a full-scale survey in the same venue (2023). While the initial articles may appear more survey-like, this extensive survey could have been positioned as a standard survey paper; however, given the significant amount of new theoretical work presented, we deemed it appropriate to include these novel contributions within the survey.

the Soret effect in mixtures of water and alcohol (1-propanol and 2-ethylhexanol). Our results demonstrate that water migrates toward the hot spot regardless of the specific alcohol type, though with varying magnitudes. We evaluated two molecular models for water and developed corresponding mixture potentials for both symmetric and asymmetric systems. Although the Lennard-Jones parameters and cross-interaction strengths were adjusted using experimental densities and heats of mixing, the simulated thermal diffusion factors diverge significantly from experimental data. This discrepancy suggests the need for additional refinement terms in the cross-interaction potentials or indicates a limitation in the linear approximation of the concentration Soret effect. Additionally, we analyzed the auto-correlation functions of the energy components for water and found that the algebraic average yields a thermal diffusion factor consistent with experimental results, further supporting the validity of the concentration approximation. Finally, we investigated the molecular-scale mechanisms driving these phenomena. We computed the partial contribution of each component to the total excess heat flux and constructed a phase diagram to assess the impact of density and composition fluctuations on these contributions. The analysis reveals that the fluctuation term arising from the cross-correlation of heat flux components is dominant in driving the Soret effect in alcohol-water mixtures. We also examined the composition dependence of these fluctuation terms to explain the observed variations in the Soret effect across different mixtures. For alcohol-water systems, the dominant fluctuation terms are linked to the composition dependence of the cross-correlation terms between translational and rotational kinetic energy components. We found that the contribution of these fluctuations to the Soret effect is not uniform; it varies depending on the specific alcohol used. This variation correlates with the asymmetry in the structural organization of water molecules within the mixture. In symmetric mixtures, these fluctuations stem from the reorganization of alcohol molecules, whereas in asymmetric mixtures, they are driven by the reorganization of water molecules. We attribute this to the different contributions of each molecule's reorganization to the overall structure and composition fluctuations. These findings may aid in clarifying the molecular mechanisms of the Soret effect and provide a foundation for future theoretical approaches. Keywords: Soret effect; Alcohol-water mixtures; Heat flux fluctuations; Structural organization. (DOI: 10.1063/5.0002500)

However, the vast number of reactions and species involved makes it impossible to possess complete rate information within a reasonable timeframe. Consequently, chemical models frequently incorporate approximate or guessed values to address unknown reactions and fill data gaps. This paper examines the impact of rate uncertainties on chemical modeling outcomes, specifically regarding the production of key molecules and isotopologues. By employing Monte Carlo simulations to introduce uncertainties into rate coefficients, we demonstrate that resulting molecular abundances can deviate from standard model predictions by several orders of magnitude. To quantify the probability distribution of these abundances, we utilize the Monte Carlo method, which involves randomly varying rate coefficients and generating a distribution of abundance distributions. We applied this approach to a model of protostellar gas and a diffuse cloud model, calculating abundance distributions for H$_2$O, NH$_3$, $^{13}$C$_2$H$_2$, and $^{13}$CH$_3$CN. Furthermore, we developed a computational algorithm to identify the rate coefficients most significantly influencing a specific molecular abundance, allowing us to pinpoint the interactions responsible for variations in abundance distributions. This methodology can be easily adapted for other molecules and astronomical objects. Ultimately, we conclude that uncertainties in rate coefficients significantly affect output distributions in both protostellar and diffuse cloud chemical models, and that the Monte Carlo technique serves as a valuable tool for characterizing these outputs and guiding future rate measurements. Future work will extend this approach to other molecules, diffuse and protostellar gas models, and models for other astronomical objects. Additionally, we propose applying the Monte Carlo method to derive abundance distributions for molecules and isotopologues in interstellar gas and protostellar envelopes based on observed abundances and rate uncertainties, and eventually comparing these derived abundances with actual observations. This strategy could assist in determining rate coefficients required to accurately model chemical models and align them with actual observations. The Monte Carlo method is also being utilized to determine the abundance and composition of cometary material. Consequently, we propose that data-relevant information is a more precise guiding principle for transformations. This approach aims to train a model using data from various sources so it can generalize to new tasks with minimal additional learning. Consequently, meta-learning has become a primary strategy for addressing small and zero-shot scenarios in learning-from-data frameworks. Driven by the need for generalizable models, this paper investigates whether meta-learning offers advantages in predicting drug-target interactions. Using the DG-INT database, we gathered interactions involving diverse drug classes and targets. We employed the popular multi-task learning architecture DeepFeature to multi-task predict interactions between drug pairs featuring similar chemistry. Our findings indicate that models trained on large datasets demonstrate superior performance with transfer learning, though they struggle to generalize to drugs with distinct chemistry. Additionally, we observed that predicting interactions between similar targets yields more accurate results, likely due to the higher homogeneity of such datasets. Overall, while current methods face challenges generalizing to novel drugs and targets, both feature engineering and meta-learning emerge as promising avenues for future research in drug prediction. Although the concept of legal personhood for robots is frequently proposed as a solution, it remains highly contentious and would demand significant societal shifts. This paper presents an alternative approach inspired by the concept of 'legal exposure'—the ability to bear legal obligations—as an intermediate step between mere machine intelligence and full legal personhood. Conventional methods typically separate speech recognition (ASR) and machine translation (MT), yet such pipelines often result in information loss and increased computational costs. Although recent research has explored directly pipeline-free end-to-end (EE2E) ST methods, these approaches struggle with low-resource language pairs and face difficulties in aligning speech and text effectively. To address these challenges, this study introduces a hierarchical model that leverages cross-modal alignment to generate ST output. The architecture consists of two primary components: a speech-to-text (S2T) module that converts audio into target-language characters, and a character-to-text (C2T) module that transforms these characters into final target text. The S2T module and the initial C2T stage are trained using an ST task loss, while the remaining C2T stages are trained to maximize the Intersection over Union (IoU) between the model's output and ground-truth text during training. Additionally, the proposed method integrates a multi-branch unit that aligns speech and text features to construct a more accurate joint speech-text representation, which then guides the subsequent C2T stages. Extensive experiments on IWSLT 17/18 and WMT 19 datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves +2.32 / +1.94 BLEU score improvements over strong baseline models on low-resource English-to-target translations and +0.48 / +0.48 improvements on highly-resourced French-to-German and Chinese-English translations, respectively. Memorable paths are identified as the carlier-than-or-equal-to solutions for this extended model, while recallable paths are defined as the later-than-or-equal-to ones. Carlier-than-or-equal-to memorable paths for the standard heat equation are derived both theoretically and numerically. Furthermore, two distinct but related concepts of local and global smoothness—corresponding to absolute and relative differentiability—are introduced for general memorable paths. It is demonstrated that both properties hold for paths satisfying the standard heat equation if and only if the path functions are continuously differentiable. Finally, the four paths that are simultaneously memorable and recallable, corresponding to the standard heat equation and classified as such, are identified as "the most reasonable paths." Their relative and absolute differentiability is proven. Furthermore, the Carlier-Smith criterion for relative differentiability is established for general memorable paths, and a necessary and sufficient condition for absolute differentiability, which is both simple and effective for distinguishing between two such paths, is provided. The paths' compliance with the heat conduction differential equation is also examined. Specifically, the difference between the memorable path's solution and that of the heat conduction equation is shown to be infinitely differentiable. Finally, the concept of "the most reasonable temperature" is formally defined for the classical problem of continuous, absolute, and relative differentiability, with the relative and absolute differentiability of the memorable path's temperature solution established. Finally, the relationship between memorable paths and the maximum entropy principle is explored. It is shown that the memorable path's temperature solution maximizes the entropy functional, provided the initial and boundary conditions are sufficiently regular and the memorable path's memorable "cause" is sufficiently smooth. Conversely, the initial and boundary conditions are demonstrated to be sufficiently regular if the memorable path's "effect" is sufficiently smooth. Finally, the relative and absolute differentiability of the memorable path's "cause" is established as sufficient to guarantee the validity of the maximum entropy principle for the memorable path's temperature solution. Spring actuators enable legged locomotion robots to achieve high-performance and energy-efficient movements. Experiments show that this modified feedback controller effectively tracks optimized trajectories over a range of walking speeds during free and guided dynamic walking. Lett. 90, 079801, 2003), which provides criteria for the minimal eigenvalues of Hermitian matrices formed from the state's density matrix. We demonstrate that this approach remains viable even when given access only to a variational quantum cohering operation (VQCO)—a simplified representation of the full density matrix. Consequently, our findings are applicable to scenarios utilizing hypothetical measurement devices capable of state reconstruction limited to the third-order moment matrix. Finally, we present experimental data confirming that the VSV successfully identifies separable states across systems of up to six qubits. Furthermore, these results indicate that the VSV can distinguish between separable and entangled states of four-qubit systems with approximately equal probability. The VSV serves as a practical tool for experimentally determining the separability of quantum states in small-scale multi-qubit systems. Additionally, it establishes a foundation for developing VQA-based strategies to set bounds on the distance of unknown states from the set of separable states. Such bounded distance metrics are valuable for quantifying entanglement in systems where generating the complete density matrix is infeasible. To validate the efficacy of the VSV, we propose a figure of merit (FoM) that averages the algorithm's performance on both separable and entangled states. This FoM peaks when the state is either purely separable or maximally entangled. We find that the foM reaches its maximum value when estimating the density matrix is restricted to the lower half of the third-order moment matrix. These insights are expected to aid in designing more effective VSV protocols within quantum information processing experiments. Our proposal holds promise for distinguishing the separability of quantum states in small quantum systems accessible in the near future. We anticipate that the VSV will facilitate greater insight into the separation capabilities of quantum devices and enhance the characterization of quantum states in small quantum systems. The VSV will also enable researchers to establish bounds on the distance between quantum states and the set of separable states. These distance bounds are particularly useful because they provide rigorous limits on entanglement without requiring the full density matrix. This approach is especially relevant when considering the trade-off between the resources required to measure the entire density matrix and the benefits gained from these distance bounds. The model incorporates finite and field-aligned ion mean free paths; under the conditions of $k_\perp \lambda_{e\perp} \ll 1$ and $k_z \lambda_{e\parallel} \ll 1$, electron and ion dynamics exhibit distinct behaviors based on their respective length scales and associated Debye and Braginskii lengths. In the electron sector, a tearing mode characterized by $k_z \ll k_\perp$ emerges, whereas in the ion sector, a drift-Alfvén mode with $k_z \ll k_\perp$ is established. Consequently, a hybrid drift-tearing mode arises in the system, displaying $k_\parallel \ll k_\perp$ in a broad parameter range extending to the limit of $k_\parallel \sim k_\perp$. Analytical growth rates for the hybrid drift-tearing mode are derived and compared with results from numerical code. It is demonstrated that a sufficiently long field-aligned system can stabilize a microtearing mode characterized by $k_\perp \lambda_{e\perp} \ll 1$ in the pure electron model, whereas the stability of the hybrid drift-tearing mode remains independent of the field-aligned system size. Furthermore, it is shown that the threshold on the normalized perpendicular electron mean free path required for the microtearing instability varies significantly with $k_\perp$ across different parameter regimes. Specifically, the threshold increases monotonically with $k_\perp$ in the short-wavelength regime but exhibits a sharp decrease in the long-wavelength regime. These findings indicate that $\lambda_{e\perp}$ plays a critical role in determining the threshold $s_{m\perp}^{1/2}$ for the microtearing instability, alongside the normalized parallel length. Finally, the findings are validated using a 2D PIC code, with results aligning well with the analytical growth rates for short-wavelength and long-wavelength regimes. It is concluded that the short-wavelength and long-wavelength microtearing modes exhibit fundamentally distinct characteristics, driven by the finite size of the $\rho_e$ surface current. This study represents a significant advancement in the understanding of microtearing modes, with potential applications to helicon sources, ICRF heated plasmas, and ion cyclotron heating of tokamaks. To enhance user experience, these systems aim to return results that precisely match user intent; however, delivering such accurate results is challenging due to inherent ambiguities in visual search queries. To address this, we introduce a novel interactive framework designed to refine the visual interpretation of a query and ultimately present more relevant final results to the user. Our focus is on scenarios where users seek a specific object instance within a known class. We formulate this specific visual interpretation as a supervised learning challenge and develop a new interface class known as the Visual Similarity Similarity (VSS) widget. The VSS widget allows users to input the specific attributes they wish to find by defining the desired characteristics of the object. We present a unified architecture for the widget's graphical user interface, ensuring consistent core functionalities. This approach facilitates the creation of increasingly accurate query interpretations, producing intermediate results that help users refine their search and arrive at final outcomes highly aligned with their intentions. We formally specify the widget and its operations to establish a common interface for implementing and evaluating enhanced interactive visual object retrieval systems. We initially define the operational steps and evaluate the widget's effectiveness in improving result relevance through a series of experiments. Additionally, we analyze the widget's impact on both visual interpretation and overall relevance across various existing retrieval systems. Our experimental findings indicate consistent improvements in result relevance when the VSS widget is integrated. These experiments also highlight the widget's significant impact on visual interpretation, demonstrating that integrating it with multiple systems yields interpretable intermediate results. Finally, we examine the widget's performance in cold-start scenarios. Our results show consistent performance gains when the widget is employed to progressively refine visual queries. These experiments confirm the widget's capability to effectively interpret and address visual search queries regarding visual object instances. We believe this case study contributes to advancing the state of the art in interactive visual object retrieval. The widget implementation is available at https://github.com/ibm-iis/VSS-Widget. Within these theories, geometric components function as non-Riemannian connections that drive the renormalization group evolution of physical parameters. A prominent example is the semi-symmetric connection, defined by the condition $\mathrm{R}^\alpha_{\beta\gamma\delta}\mathrm{g}_{\alpha\delta}=Q_{\beta\gamma}$, where $Q_{\beta\gamma}$ represents a matrix field. This study examines a scalar-field theory of semi-symmetric gravity to examine symmetry breaking mechanisms. Furthermore, we derive the renormalization group beta functions for the matrix amplitudes, analyzing their asymptotic behavior to determine the spontaneous breaking of global and gauge symmetries in scenarios involving both real and complex scalar fields. In the $\phi^4$ limit of the scalar-field model, we successfully reproduce results from standard relativistic field theory. Finally, we highlight that these theories may exhibit rich behavior at finite temperatures and establish a natural framework for analyzing symmetry breaking within condensed matter systems. Consequently, scalar-field theories based on semi-symmetric gravity hold potential applicability in modeling symmetries in condensed matter physics. networks, this research investigates the deployment of reception-transmission switching (RTS) within cognitive non-transmission capable (NTC) networks. By allowing multiple NTC nodes to share a single reception point equipped with high-quality radio measurements, RTS enhances the transmission capabilities of NTC nodes. We formulate an optimization problem aimed at maximizing the sum-rate of all users, which accounts for maximum achievable rates, WiFi interference, and the relay gain associated with each NTC node. Due to the computational intractability of this problem, we introduce a novel cognitive multi-user setup where NTC nodes alternately adopt either a transmissive or non-transmissive mode, defined by whether their users transmit through the RTS or directly. Leveraging the specific traits of the WiFi environment, we develop a deep learning (DL)-based strategy to determine the RTS configuration and transmission schedules for all users at each time step. Our results demonstrate that the DL-based scheme achieves performance closely matching the optimal solution. Furthermore, we observe that the sum-rate for NTC nodes increases with the presence of NTC nodes, whereas traditional WiFi users experience reduced sum-rates due to sharing the reception point. Finally, we analyze the trade-off between sum-rate performance and computational complexity. Experimental data indicates that sum-rates can improve by up to 200% through RTS, with the proposed DL-based scheme incurring additional time-complexity costs of approximately 10, 20, and 50 microseconds for small, medium, and large-scale networks, respectively. These findings confirm the effectiveness of the RTS concept, highlighting its potential to enable scalable WiFi communication for future smart home environments.
